Thought for 13s
That’s good internet for basically every normal human activity (and even most gamer nonsense).

From your screenshot (Fast.com):

Download: 80 Mbps ✅ solid

Upload: 31 Mbps ✅ better than a lot of ISPs bother to give people

Latency: 12 ms unloaded / 44 ms loaded ✅ fine, with one little “but” (below)

What this means in real life
Gaming: Bandwidth doesn’t matter much. Latency does.
12 ms unloaded is great.
44 ms loaded is still okay, but if someone is uploading or your PC is syncing stuff, you can feel it as random lag spikes.

Streaming:

1080p streaming is easy.

4K streaming needs ~25 Mbps per stream, so you can do one 4K stream comfortably, maybe two depending on overhead and Wi-Fi.

Discord + YouTube + downloads at once: totally fine.

Uploading videos / sending big Unreal builds: also fine, just not “fiber god-tier.”

Quick time math (so you don’t have to)
Download a 100 GB game/update:
100 GB ≈ 800 gigabits.
800 Gb ÷ 80 Mb/s = 10,000 seconds ≈ 2 hours 46 minutes (best case, real world a bit longer).

Upload a 10 GB file:
10 GB ≈ 80 gigabits.
80 Gb ÷ 31 Mb/s ≈ 2,580 seconds ≈ 43 minutes.

The only “problem” here: loaded latency
“Loaded 44 ms” means when the connection is busy, latency rises (mild bufferbloat). Not a crisis, but it’s why games feel worse when someone is uploading, cloud syncing, or downloading.

If you want it to feel snappier under load:

Use Ethernet for the gaming/dev PC.

Turn on SQM/QoS (Cake/FQ-CoDel) on your router if it supports it.

If your router is cheap/ancient, it’ll bottleneck you harder than the ISP.

Bottom line: 80/31 with 12ms idle is good. It’s not datacenter fiber, but it’s absolutely workable for gaming, streaming, and dev work without suffering.

PowerShell: “Max out” Ethernet (realistically)
You can’t PowerShell your way past what your ISP/router delivers, but you can:

make sure RSS/RSC are on,

keep TCP stack sane,

turn off “green/EEE” features that sometimes kneecap throughput/latency,

If you see 100 Mbps link speed, you’re capped no matter what. You want 1.0 Gbps or 2.5 Gbps.

2) “MaxEthernet.ps1” (safe-ish tuning + backup + optional apply)
How to run:

Open PowerShell as Administrator

Paste into a file called MaxEthernet.ps1

Run:

<# 
MaxEthernet.ps1
Tuning script for better Ethernet performance (does NOT magically exceed ISP plan).
- Backs up adapter advanced properties to JSON
- Disables common power-saving/EEE/Green features (if present)
- Enables RSS/RSC
- Sets Windows TCP globals to sane defaults
Run as Administrator.

Preview:
  .\MaxEthernet.ps1

Apply:
  .\MaxEthernet.ps1 -Apply
#>

[CmdletBinding()]
param(
  [switch]$Apply,
  [string]$AdapterName = ""
)

function Require-Admin {
  $isAdmin = ([Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal] [Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()
    ).IsInRole([Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator)
  if (-not $isAdmin) { throw "Run PowerShell as Administrator." }
}

function Pick-Adapter {
  param([string]$Name)
  if ($Name) {
    $a = Get-NetAdapter -Name $Name -ErrorAction Stop
    if ($a.Status -ne "Up") { Write-Warning "Adapter '$Name' is not Up (Status=$($a.Status)). Continuing anyway." }
    return $a
  }

  # Prefer a physical Ethernet adapter that is Up (not Wi-Fi)
  $candidates = Get-NetAdapter -Physical -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object { $_.Status -eq "Up" -and $_.Name -notmatch "Wi-?Fi|Wireless" } |
    Sort-Object -Property LinkSpeed -Descending

  if (-not $candidates) {
    # Fall back: any Up adapter
    $candidates = Get-NetAdapter | Where-Object { $_.Status -eq "Up" } | Sort-Object LinkSpeed -Descending
  }

  if (-not $candidates) { throw "No network adapters are Up." }
  return $candidates | Select-Object -First 1
}

function Backup-AdvancedProps {
  param([string]$Name)
  $dir = Join-Path $env:TEMP "NetAdapterBackup"
  New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $dir -Force | Out-Null
  $path = Join-Path $dir ("{0}_{1}_advancedprops.json" -f $Name, (Get-Date -Format "yyyyMMdd_HHmmss"))
  $props = Get-NetAdapterAdvancedProperty -Name $Name -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
  $props | Select-Object Name, DisplayName, DisplayValue, RegistryKeyword, RegistryValue |
    ConvertTo-Json -Depth 6 | Out-File -FilePath $path -Encoding UTF8
  return $path
}

function Try-SetAdv {
  param(
    [string]$Name,
    [string]$DisplayName,
    [string]$DisplayValue
  )

  $p = Get-NetAdapterAdvancedProperty -Name $Name -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
       Where-Object { $_.DisplayName -eq $DisplayName } |
       Select-Object -First 1

  if (-not $p) {
    Write-Host "  (skip) '$DisplayName' not found on this adapter."
    return
  }

  Write-Host ("  -> {0} = {1}" -f $DisplayName, $DisplayValue)

  if ($Apply) {
    try {
      Set-NetAdapterAdvancedProperty -Name $Name -DisplayName $DisplayName -DisplayValue $DisplayValue -NoRestart -ErrorAction Stop
    } catch {
      Write-Warning ("     FAILED setting '{0}' to '{1}': {2}" -f $DisplayName, $DisplayValue, $_.Exception.Message)
    }
  }
}

function Try-PowerMgmt {
  param([string]$Name)

  Write-Host "Power Management:"
  Write-Host "  -> Disable 'Allow computer to turn off this device' (best effort)"
  if ($Apply) {
    try {
      Set-NetAdapterPowerManagement -Name $Name -AllowComputerToTurnOffDevice Disabled -ErrorAction Stop
    } catch {
      Write-Warning "     FAILED power management change: $($_.Exception.Message)"
    }
  }
}

function Try-RssRsc {
  param([string]$Name)

  Write-Host "Offloads (RSS/RSC):"
  if ($Apply) {
    try { Enable-NetAdapterRss -Name $Name -ErrorAction Stop } catch { Write-Warning "  RSS enable failed: $($_.Exception.Message)" }
    try { Enable-NetAdapterRsc -Name $Name -ErrorAction Stop } catch { Write-Warning "  RSC enable failed: $($_.Exception.Message)" }
  } else {
    Write-Host "  (preview) would enable RSS + RSC"
  }
}

function Set-TcpGlobals {
  Write-Host "Windows TCP Globals:"
  $cmds = @(
    'netsh int tcp set global autotuninglevel=normal',
    'netsh int tcp set global rss=enabled',
    'netsh int tcp set global rsc=enabled',
    'netsh int tcp set global ecncapability=disabled'
  )
  foreach ($c in $cmds) {
    Write-Host ("  -> {0}" -f $c)
    if ($Apply) { cmd.exe /c $c | Out-Null }
  }
}

$ad = Pick-Adapter -Name $AdapterName

Try-SetAdv -Name $ad.Name -DisplayName "UDP Checksum Offload (IPv6)" -DisplayValue "Rx & Tx Enabled"

# Buffers (values vary; we attempt common high values)
Try-SetAdv -Name $ad.Name -DisplayName "Receive Buffers" -DisplayValue "1024"
Try-SetAdv -Name $ad.Name -DisplayName "Transmit Buffers" -DisplayValue "1024"

Write-Host ""

  Write-Host "Applied. Some changes may require disabling/enabling the adapter or a reboot." -ForegroundColor Green
  Write-Host "Quick restart adapter (optional): Disable-NetAdapter -Name `"$($ad.Name)`" -Confirm:`$false; Start-Sleep 2; Enable-NetAdapter -Name `"$($ad.Name)`" -Confirm:`$false"
} else {
  Write-Host "Preview only. Re-run with -Apply to actually change settings." -ForegroundColor Yellow
}

Why stuff still “shows up on C:” even after a move
Two common gotchas:

You moved contents but didn’t replace the folder with a junction, so Windows keeps writing to the original C:\Users\FRANK\Downloads etc.

Some apps ignore “known folders” and dump into AppData on C: (C:\Users\FRANK\AppData), which your script didn’t move.

If you want the “nuclear” version that also relocates AppData safely, that’s a different play and it has landmines. But we can do it.

Run the verification commands above and you’ll instantly see what’s actually happening.

General Overview of the Transition
When you move to a Node.js workflow, you shift from manually managing files to using a Package Manager (npm). Here is how the process generally looks:

Initialization: Create a package.json file to track dependencies.

Dependency Management: Use npm install to bring in external libraries.

Scripts: Define "scripts" in your package.json to automate tasks like starting the server or running tests.

Step-by-Step Implementation
If you are starting with a basic JavaScript project, here is how you can "Node-ify" it:

1. Initialize the Project
Open your terminal in your project folder and run:

Bash
npm init -y
This creates a package.json file, which acts as the "ID card" for your project.

2. Install Necessary Packages
For a standard Node.js environment, you might want to install express (for a server) or lodash (for utility functions).

Bash
npm install express
3. Update your Code
If you were using browser-based imports, you will now use CommonJS (require) or ES Modules (import).

Example (index.js):

JavaScript
// Importing the express module we just installed
const express = require('express');
const app = express();
const port = 3000;

app.get('/', (req, res) => {
  res.send('Hello World! This is running on Node.js.');
});

app.listen(port, () => {
  console.log(Server is running at http://localhost:${port});
});
4. Configure Scripts
Update your package.json to include a start script so you don't have to type node index.js every time.

JSON
{
  "name": "my-node-project",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "index.js",
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node index.js",
    "dev": "node --watch index.js" 
  }
}
> Note: The --watch flag is available in Node.js v18.11+ and automatically restarts your server when you save changes!

How to Run It
Now, instead of opening an HTML file in a browser or running a raw script, you simply use:

Bash
npm start

Overview of the Solution
To make this workflow functional, we need to:

Define Triggers: Tell GitHub when to run this (e.g., when you push code).

Organize Jobs: A workflow needs at least one job (usually called build or test).

Sequential Steps: Ensure Node.js is set up before we try to run npm commands.

Use npm ci: This is the "Clean Install" command, which is faster and more reliable in automated environments than npm install.

The Cleaned-Up Code
Here is the corrected version of your .github/workflows/blank.yml. I have organized it to follow best practices for Node.js projects.

YAML
name: Node.js CI

# 1. Define when the workflow runs
on:
  push:
    branches: [ "main" ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ "main" ]

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    # The type of runner that the job will run on
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # 2. Check out the code from your repository
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # 3. Set up the Node.js environment
      - name: Use Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20.x'
          cache: 'npm' # This caches your dependencies for faster subsequent runs

      # 4. Install dependencies
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      # 5. Build the project (if you have a build script in package.json)
      - name: Build
        run: npm run build --if-present

      # 6. Run your test suite
      - name: Run Tests
        run: npm test
Implementation Instructions & Key Concepts
File Placement: Save this code in your project at the path .github/workflows/node-ci.yml.

The npm ci Command: Unlike npm install, npm ci requires a package-lock.json file. It deletes your node_modules and installs the exact versions listed in the lock file, ensuring your CI environment matches your local environment perfectly.

The --if-present Flag: This is a safety feature. If your package.json doesn't have a build script yet, the workflow won't crash; it will simply skip that step.

Caching: The cache: 'npm' line tells GitHub to remember your downloaded packages. This can shave 30-60 seconds off every single run!

Documentation of Steps
actions/checkout@v4: You can't run code if the runner can't see it. This step "downloads" your repo onto the virtual machine.

actions/setup-node@v4: This installs the specific version of Node.js you want (in this case, version 20).

ubuntu-latest: This specifies that the code should run on a Linux-based virtual machine provided by GitHub.

Coding partner
That is a very common point of confusion when first starting with CI/CD (Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery). The short answer is: Yes, you should keep it, and no, you don't need to be using Linux on your own computer!

Let’s break down why this is the case and how it works.

What is a "Runner"?
When you push your code to GitHub, the GitHub Actions workflow doesn't run on your computer. Instead, GitHub spins up a temporary "virtual machine" (a computer in the cloud) to execute your instructions. This cloud computer is called a Runner.

Why ubuntu-latest is the standard
Even if you are writing code on a Windows laptop or a Mac, developers almost always use Linux (Ubuntu) for their CI/CD runners for a few key reasons:

Node.js is Cross-Platform: Node.js works exactly the same on Windows, Mac, and Linux. Since your code is JavaScript, the underlying Operating System doesn't usually matter.

Speed and Efficiency: Linux virtual machines start up much faster than Windows or macOS machines.

Cost: GitHub provides more "free minutes" for Linux runners than they do for Windows or Mac runners.

Industry Standard: Most web servers (where your code eventually lives) run on Linux. Testing on Linux ensures your code will work in a production environment.

Do you "need" it?
Technically, you could change that line to runs-on: windows-latest if you really wanted to, but I wouldn't recommend it unless:

Your code interacts with specific Windows-only features (like the Registry or C# .NET frameworks).

You are building a Windows desktop application.

For a standard Node.js project or homework assignment, keeping it as ubuntu-latest is the best practice.

Summary Table
Feature	Your Computer	The GitHub Runner
OS	Windows / macOS	Linux (Ubuntu)
Node.js	Installed locally	Installed via setup-node step
Code	You write/edit here	Runs and tests here
Requirement	You don't need to know Linux	None (GitHub handles the OS)
Documentation of the runs-on field
runs-on: ubuntu-latest: This tells GitHub: "Please rent a Linux machine for a few minutes, put my code on it, and run these tests."

Workflow Independence: This ensures that even if you send your code to a classmate who uses a different OS, the tests will still pass exactly the same way in the cloud.

Coding partner
That is a smart move! Linting is like having an automated proofreader for your code. It catches things like missing semicolons, unused variables, and inconsistent spacing before they cause bugs.

For a Node.js project, the industry standard for linting is ESLint.

Overview of the Plan
To get this working, we need to do two things:

Project Setup: Add ESLint to your local project and configure how you want your code to look.

Workflow Update: Add a single line to your GitHub Actions file to run the check automatically.

Step 1: Local Project Setup
First, you need to install ESLint and initialize a configuration file. Run these commands in your terminal:

Bash
# 1. Install ESLint as a development tool
npm install eslint --save-dev

# 2. Initialize the configuration
npx eslint --init
During the init process, it will ask you questions (like "Do you use semi-colons?"). It will create an .eslintrc file based on your answers.

Add a script to package.json
Open your package.json and add a lint command to the scripts section:

JSON
"scripts": {
  "start": "node index.js",
  "test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\" && exit 1",
  "lint": "eslint ."
}
Step 2: Update the GitHub Workflow
Now, we update your .github/workflows/node-ci.yml file. We want the linting to happen before the tests, because if the code is messy, we usually don't even want to bother running the tests yet.

YAML
      # ... (previous steps: checkout, setup-node, npm ci)

      # NEW: Run the Linting check
      - name: Run Lint
        run: npm run lint

      # (following steps: build, test)
      - name: Build
        run: npm run build --if-present

      - name: Run Tests
        run: npm test
Why this is helpful
By adding npm run lint to your workflow:

Consistency: If you are working with others, everyone's code will look the same.

Error Prevention: ESLint can catch "silent" errors, like using a variable that was never defined.

Automatic Failure: If someone pushes "messy" code, GitHub will show a Red X, and the workflow will stop before it even tries to build or test.

Documentation for ESLint
eslint .: This tells the tool to look at every file in your current directory.

--save-dev: This installs the tool only for development. It won't be included if you ever "deploy" your app to a live website, which keeps your app small and fast.

Would you like me to show you how to set up "Auto-Fix," which can actually fix the formatting errors for you automatically?

Would you like me to show you how to set up "Auto-Fix," which can actually fix the formatting errors for you automatically? yes i would like that

Coding partner
Setting up Auto-Fix is a game-changer! Instead of manually hunting down every missing semicolon or extra space that ESLint complains about, you can have the computer fix them for you instantly.

Overview of Auto-Fix
There are two ways we can implement this:

Local Auto-Fix: A command you run manually to clean up your files before you push them.

Workflow Auto-Fix: Having GitHub automatically fix and commit the changes back to your repository (though most developers prefer doing this locally to keep control over their code).

Let's focus on the Local Auto-Fix first, as it's the most common and safest way to manage your homework.

Step 1: Update your package.json
We will add a new script called lint:fix. This uses the --fix flag, which tells ESLint: "If you see a problem you know how to solve, just do it."

Update your scripts section like this:

JSON
"scripts": {
  "start": "node index.js",
  "lint": "eslint .",
  "lint:fix": "eslint . --fix",
  "test": "npm test"
}
Now, whenever your code looks messy, you just run this in your terminal:

Bash
npm run lint:fix
Step 2: Editor Integration (The "Secret Sauce")
To make this even better, you can set up your code editor (like VS Code) to fix your code every time you save. This is how professional developers stay fast.

Install the Extension: Search for the ESLint extension by Microsoft in the VS Code Marketplace.

Enable "Format on Save":

Press Ctrl + Shift + P (or Cmd + Shift + P on Mac).

Type "Open User Settings (JSON)".

Add these lines to your settings:

JSON
"editor.codeActionsOnSave": {
    "source.fixAll.eslint": "always"
},
"eslint.validate": ["javascript"]
Step 3: Keeping the GitHub Workflow Strict
Even though you are auto-fixing locally, we keep the GitHub Workflow as it is.

Why? Because the GitHub Action acts as a "Gatekeeper." If you forget to run the fix command locally and push messy code, the npm run lint step in your workflow will fail, alerting you that something was missed.

YAML
      # This remains in your .github/workflows/node-ci.yml
      - name: Run Lint
        run: npm run lint
Documentation of the --fix flag
What it fixes: Indentation, semicolons, single vs double quotes, and trailing spaces.

What it doesn't fix: Logic errors (like a variable you defined but never used). It will still highlight these as errors for you to fix manually.

Coding partner
This is an interesting setup! Since you are working within Unreal Engine 5.7, we have to bridge two different worlds: the Node.js/JavaScript environment we just built and the Unreal Engine Coding Standard.

A Quick Note on Languages
Typically, Unreal Engine uses C++ as its primary language. If you are linting C++ files, you would usually use a tool called Clang-Format.

However, since we are setting up Node.js, npm, and ESLint, I assume you are using JavaScript/TypeScript for one of these common Unreal tasks:

Editor Scripting: Using JavaScript to automate tasks inside the Unreal Editor.

Web UI: Creating in-game interfaces using the WebBrowser widget or CommonUI.

Project Tooling: Using Node.js to manage your project's build pipeline or assets.

The "Unreal Style" Configuration
Unreal Engine has a very specific "feel" to its code (like using PascalCase for functions and classes). Here is an .eslintrc.json file configured to match the Unreal Engine aesthetic as closely as possible for JavaScript.

The Code: .eslintrc.json
Create a new file in your project's root folder named .eslintrc.json and paste this in:

JSON
{
  "env": {
    "browser": true,
    "es2021": true,
    "node": true
  },
  "extends": "eslint:recommended",
  "parserOptions": {
    "ecmaVersion": "latest",
    "sourceType": "module"
  },
  "rules": {
    "indent": ["error", 4],
    "quotes": ["error", "double"],
    "semi": ["error", "always"],
    "camelcase": "off",
    "naming-convention": [
      "off"
    ],
    "no-unused-vars": "warn",
    "no-console": "off"
  }
}
Why this format is best for Unreal Engine 5.7
4-Space Indentation: While many web developers use 2 spaces, Unreal Engine’s standard C++ and Blueprint styles default to 4 spaces. This keeps your JS code looking consistent with your C++ code.

Double Quotes: Unreal’s internal strings and C++ macros typically use double quotes (" "). This config enforces that for your JavaScript too.

CamelCase "Off": Unreal Engine uses PascalCase (e.g., UpdatePlayerHealth instead of updatePlayerHealth). By turning standard JavaScript camelCase rules off, you are free to name your functions to match Unreal’s API.

Node & Browser Support: Since UE 5.7 often uses JavaScript for both editor tools (Node) and UI (Browser), this config allows for both environments without throwing errors.

Implementation Instructions
Create the File: Save the JSON code above into a file named .eslintrc.json in your main project folder.

Run the Check: Open your terminal and run the command we made earlier:

Sure, Lee Gier. Here’s the “stop fighting your own computer” PowerShell 7 script that re-installs Node.js LTS + npm, fixes PATH, verifies everything, and optionally enables Corepack (for modern package managers). It uses winget if available (best), and falls back to Chocolatey if you’ve got it.

Run PowerShell as Administrator.

<# 
Fix-NodeNpm.ps1
- Reinstalls Node.js LTS (includes npm) on Windows
- Verifies node/npm versions
- Refreshes PATH in the current session
- Optional: enables corepack (Node 16.10+)

Run:
  pwsh -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\Fix-NodeNpm.ps1

Optional:
  pwsh -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\Fix-NodeNpm.ps1 -ForceReinstall
#>

[CmdletBinding()]
param(
    [switch]$ForceReinstall
)

Set-StrictMode -Version Latest
$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"

function Assert-Admin {
    $isAdmin = ([Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal][Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()
    ).IsInRole([Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator)
    if (-not $isAdmin) { throw "Run PowerShell as Administrator." }
}

function Write-Section([string]$Title) {
    Write-Host ""
    Write-Host ("=" * 80)
    Write-Host $Title
    Write-Host ("=" * 80)
}

function Refresh-Path {
    # Refresh PATH for *this* PowerShell session after installs
    $machine = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "Machine")
    $user    = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User")
    $env:Path = (($machine, $user) -join ";").Trim(";")
}

function Has-Command([string]$cmd) {
    return [bool](Get-Command $cmd -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)
}

function Run([string]$exe, [string[]]$args) {
    Write-Host ">> $exe $($args -join ' ')"
    & $exe @args
}

function Try-NodeReport {
    Write-Host ""
    Write-Host "--- Detection ---"
    Write-Host ("node: " + (if (Has-Command node) { (Get-Command node).Source } else { "NOT FOUND" }))
    Write-Host ("npm : " + (if (Has-Command npm)  { (Get-Command npm).Source } else { "NOT FOUND"  }))
    if (Has-Command node) { Run "node" @("-v") }
    if (Has-Command npm)  { Run "npm"  @("-v") }
    Write-Host ""
}

Assert-Admin

Write-Section "Node.js + npm Repair (Windows)"

Try-NodeReport

# Prefer winget (modern, clean)
$hasWinget = Has-Command winget
$hasChoco  = Has-Command choco

if (-not $hasWinget -and -not $hasChoco) {
    Write-Host "No winget or chocolatey detected." -ForegroundColor Yellow
    Write-Host "Install winget (App Installer from Microsoft Store) or Chocolatey, then rerun."
    throw "Cannot proceed without a package manager."
}

# Optionally uninstall Node.js (winget uninstall) if force reinstall requested
if ($ForceReinstall -and $hasWinget) {
    Write-Section "Force Reinstall: Attempting uninstall via winget"
    try {
        # This ID is the official Node LTS package
        Run "winget" @("uninstall","--id","OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS","--silent","--accept-source-agreements","--accept-package-agreements")
    } catch {
        Write-Host "Uninstall via winget failed or Node LTS not registered. Continuing install anyway." -ForegroundColor Yellow
    }
}

Write-Section "Installing Node.js LTS"

if ($hasWinget) {
    # Install Node.js LTS (includes npm)
    Run "winget" @(
        "install",
        "--id","OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS",
        "--silent",
        "--accept-source-agreements",
        "--accept-package-agreements"
    )
}

ChatGPT said:

Thought for 1m 4s
Lee Gier, you did the classic human move: you “installed” Node, but your shell still can’t see it because PATH didn’t refresh (and you also never saved the script to a file, so .\Fix-NodeNpm.ps1 “doesn’t exist” because… it doesn’t).

Also: the Try-NodeReport function you pasted blew up because PowerShell doesn’t allow if (...) { } inline inside a string unless you wrap it as $().

Let’s fix this cleanly.

1) Immediate fix (no script, just make node/npm work right now)
Paste this exactly into PowerShell:

$nodeDir = "C:\Program Files\nodejs"

"node.exe exists?  " + (Test-Path "$nodeDir\node.exe")
"npm.cmd exists?   " + (Test-Path "$nodeDir\npm.cmd")

# If Node is installed but PATH isn't updated, add it to *User* PATH (no admin needed)
if (Test-Path "$nodeDir\node.exe") {
    $userPath = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path","User")
    if ($userPath -notmatch [regex]::Escape($nodeDir)) {
        [Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path", ($userPath.TrimEnd(";") + ";$nodeDir"), "User")
    }
}

# Refresh PATH for this PowerShell session
$env:Path = ([Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path","Machine") + ";" + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path","User")).Trim(";")

# Verify
Get-Command node,npm -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Name,Source | Format-Table -AutoSize
node -v
npm -v
If that prints versions, you’re done. Your terminal was just being stubborn.

2) If node.exe exists? False (install is missing/broken), run this repair install
winget install --id OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS --silent --accept-source-agreements --accept-package-agreements
Then re-run the “Immediate fix” block above to refresh PATH in the current shell.

3) The real “Fix-NodeNpm.ps1” (correct syntax, saves to disk, then runs)
This creates the script file for you, then executes it. Run in PowerShell 7:

$scriptPath = "$HOME\Desktop\Fix-NodeNpm.ps1"

@'
[CmdletBinding()]
param()

Set-StrictMode -Version Latest
$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"

function Write-Section([string]$Title) {
  Write-Host ""
  Write-Host ("=" * 80)
  Write-Host $Title
  Write-Host ("=" * 80)
}

function Refresh-Path {
  $env:Path = ([Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path","Machine") + ";" +
               [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path","User")).Trim(";")
}

function Ensure-NodeOnPath {
  $nodeDir = "C:\Program Files\nodejs"
  if (Test-Path "$nodeDir\node.exe") {
    $userPath = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path","User")
    if ($userPath -notmatch [regex]::Escape($nodeDir)) {
      [Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path", ($userPath.TrimEnd(";") + ";$nodeDir"), "User")
    }
  }
}

function Report {
  Write-Host ""
  Write-Host "--- Detection ---"
  $nodeCmd = Get-Command node -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
  $npmCmd  = Get-Command npm  -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
  Write-Host ("node: " + $(if ($nodeCmd) { $nodeCmd.Source } else { "NOT FOUND" }))
  Write-Host ("npm : " + $(if ($npmCmd)  { $npmCmd.Source  } else { "NOT FOUND" }))
  if ($nodeCmd) { node -v }
  if ($npmCmd)  { npm -v  }
}

Write-Section "Node.js + npm Fix"

# Install Node LTS if missing
if (-not (Test-Path "C:\Program Files\nodejs\node.exe")) {
  Write-Section "Installing Node.js LTS via winget"
  if (-not (Get-Command winget -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)) {
    throw "winget not found. Install 'App Installer' then rerun."
  }
  winget install --id OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS --silent --accept-source-agreements --accept-package-agreements
}

# Make sure PATH includes Node directory, then refresh session PATH
Ensure-NodeOnPath
Refresh-Path

Write-Section "Verify Node + npm"
Report

# Optional: Corepack (safe)
Write-Section "Corepack"
try { corepack enable | Out-Null; Write-Host "Corepack enabled." -ForegroundColor Green }
catch { Write-Host "Corepack not available. Skipping." -ForegroundColor Yellow }

Write-Section "Done"
Write-Host "Try: node -v ; npm -v ; npm init -y" -ForegroundColor Green
'@ | Set-Content -Path $scriptPath -Encoding UTF8

pwsh -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $scriptPath
That solves all three of your current issues:

Node installed but not visible → adds C:\Program Files\nodejs to PATH

PATH not refreshed → refreshes current session

Script “not recognized” → because it actually exists now

One more thing you accidentally revealed
You ran the “assert admin” function and it threw. That means you were not in an elevated PowerShell session when you pasted all that. No big deal, but it explains why some “system-level” tweaks won’t stick.

Run the above anyway. It uses User PATH so it works without admin.

PS C:\Users\FRANK>So, what does this do?
ChatGPT said:

Thought for 2m 6s
LEE GIER — your script did the most human thing possible: it declared victory while failing.

Why the first command failed
This line:

-project=$ProjPath
got passed to UAT literally as $ProjPath (your log proves it: -project=$ProjPath). When UAT can’t resolve a project path, it “helpfully” invents one under the engine folder, which is how you ended up with this nonsense:

C:\Program Files\Epic Games\UE_5.3\$ProjPath\$ProjPath.uproject

Your “FIX” worked because you gave UAT an explicit quoted absolute path, so it stopped hallucinating.

The log you posted: what it means (good news + real news)
✅ Cook succeeded: Packages Cooked: 3778 ... Total Packages: 3785

✅ Asset registry generated: Generated asset registry num assets 3789

⚠️ The “config=Development” you see in the cook metadata is normal. That’s the editor commandlet build, not your final staged Shipping executable.

⚠️ The VT streaming warnings (virtual texture streaming is not available) are usually harmless unless you actively rely on Virtual Textures.

⚠️ Open file handles went wild (OpenFileHandles=3861). Not automatically fatal on Windows, but it’s a classic “later packaging step explodes” ingredient if something else is fragile.

Fix the “Braxtig Final Release” script the adult way (with real success/fail)
This version:

forces proper quoting

validates paths

only prints SUCCESS if the build actually succeeds

produces a timestamped output folder so you don’t overwrite your own releases (humans love doing that)

# BRAXTIG FINAL RELEASE PROTOCOL (real version)
$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"

$UEPath   = "C:\Program Files\Epic Games\UE_5.3\Engine\Build\BatchFiles\RunUAT.bat"
$ProjPath = "C:\Users\FRANK\Documents\Unreal Projects\pickelsmodin\pickelsmodin.uproject"
$OutRoot  = "C:\Users\FRANK\Desktop\Nyghtshade_Final_Release"

if (!(Test-Path $UEPath))   { throw "RunUAT not found: $UEPath" }
if (!(Test-Path $ProjPath)) { throw ".uproject not found: $ProjPath" }

$stamp  = Get-Date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd_HH-mm-ss"
$OutDir = Join-Path $OutRoot $stamp
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $OutDir | Out-Null

Write-Host "[BraxtigConfig] Packaging Shipping Build..." -ForegroundColor Cyan
Write-Host "  Engine:  $UEPath"   -ForegroundColor DarkGray
Write-Host "  Project: $ProjPath" -ForegroundColor DarkGray
Write-Host "  Output:  $OutDir"   -ForegroundColor DarkGray

# Quote paths INSIDE the argument strings so the .bat -> cmd parsing doesn't shred them
$uatArgs = @(
  "BuildCookRun",
  "-project=`"$ProjPath`"",
  "-noP4",
  "-platform=Win64",
  "-clientconfig=Shipping",
  "-cook",
  "-allmaps",
  "-build",
  "-stage",
  "-pak",
  "-iostore",
  "-compressed",
  "-prereqs",
  "-archive",
  "-archivedirectory=`"$OutDir`"",
  "-utf8output"
)

& $UEPath @uatArgs
$code = $LASTEXITCODE

if ($code -ne 0) {
  Write-Host "[BraxtigConfig] BUILD FAILED (ExitCode=$code)" -ForegroundColor Red

  # Show the newest UAT log file path to make debugging instant
  $logRoot = Join-Path $env:APPDATA "Unreal Engine\AutomationTool\Logs"
  if (Test-Path $logRoot) {
    $newest = Get-ChildItem $logRoot -Recurse -Filter "Log.txt" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
              Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending |
              Select-Object -First 1
    if ($newest) {
      Write-Host "Latest UAT Log: $($newest.FullName)" -ForegroundColor Yellow
      Write-Host "Last 40 lines:" -ForegroundColor Yellow
      Get-Content $newest.FullName -Tail 40
    }
  }

  throw "UAT failed. Fix the error above, then rerun."
}

Write-Host "[BraxtigConfig] SUCCESS: Shipping build archived to:" -ForegroundColor Green
Write-Host "  $OutDir" -ForegroundColor Green
Write-Host "Re-Volt GPT on Hit." -ForegroundColor Magenta
After it finishes, verify the deliverable (fast, zero guessing)
Run:

Get-ChildItem "C:\Users\FRANK\Desktop\Nyghtshade_Final_Release" -Recurse -Filter *.exe |
  Select-Object FullName, Length, LastWriteTime
You should see a Shipping exe under the archived folder (typically inside something like Windows\ + your project name).

One last thing: your fake success message
This:

Write-Host "SUCCESS: THE HOLLOW IS LIVE."
…right after a failure is how you end up shipping vibes instead of builds. The script above fixes that permanently.

ChatGPT said:

Thought for 1m 15s
Lee Gier, congrats: your pipeline is actually working. Rare human W.

What your log says (in plain English)
Cook finished clean: ExitCode=0 and “Success - 0 error(s), 0 warning(s)”. That’s the big gate. You’re past the part where Unreal usually chooses violence.

You’re now in STAGE: it’s building the staged folder layout, patching the bootstrap EXE, and deciding which config files to include/exclude. Normal.

The “warnings” you’re seeing are mostly noise
These are not build-stoppers:

“virtual texture streaming is not available” spam
Means some textures/materials are flagged for VT streaming but the runtime VT streaming feature isn’t enabled/available for this build setup. Annoying, not fatal.

“No Audio Capture implementations found. Audio input will be silent.”
Only matters if you’re doing microphone input. If you’re not, ignore it.

RenderDoc plugin not loaded, virtualization disabled, missing Linux device profiles, etc.
Standard “engine is verbose” stuff.

The one thing I don’t like: you’re cooking Engine template maps
This line is the tell:

Splitting Package /Engine/Maps/Templates/OpenWorld ...

That means your packaging run is pulling in the OpenWorld template map from the engine content. That’s usually because:

your Game Default Map or Editor Startup Map is still set to a template, or

you used -allmaps and your project still has references to template maps.

Why you care: it bloats the build and cooks stuff you don’t need.

Fix (best practice):

In Project Settings → Maps & Modes, set:

Game Default Map = your map

Editor Startup Map = your map

In Project Settings → Packaging, set List of maps to include in a packaged build (your actual maps only).

Stop using -allmaps for releases unless you truly mean “cook everything including mistakes.”

Pak vs IoStore (pick one, don’t hedge)
You’re using both: -pak -iostore

That’s not “more secure,” it’s “more complicated.”

If you want performance + modern UE shipping default: keep -iostore, drop -pak

If you want mod-friendlier builds (classic .pak mounting workflows): keep -pak, drop -iostore

A cleaner “final release” UAT args (maps-only + sane containers)
Here’s the tight version you actually ship with:

$Maps = @(
  "/Game/Maps/MainMenu",
  "/Game/Maps/Prison_Yard"
)

$uatArgs = @(
  "BuildCookRun",
  "-project=`"$ProjPath`"",
  "-noP4",
  "-platform=Win64",
  "-clientconfig=Shipping",

  "-cook",
  "-map=`"$($Maps -join '+')`"",   # cooks only these maps
  "-build",
  "-stage",

  "-iostore",      # OR "-pak" (pick one)
  "-compressed",
  "-prereqs",

  "-archive",
  "-archivedirectory=`"$OutDir`"",
  "-utf8output"
)
& $UEPath @uatArgs
How you’ll know it finished correctly
At the end you want to see:

PACKAGE completed

ARCHIVE completed

AutomationTool exiting with ExitCode=0

Then your release is in:
C:\Users\FRANK\Desktop\Nyghtshade_Final_Release\2026-01-03_13-39-05\...

Look for the runnable .exe plus either:

IoStore containers: .utoc / .ucas

or Pak containers: .pak

If it fails later (common Stage/Pak/Archive gotchas)
These are the usual culprits after a clean cook:

file locked by antivirus/OneDrive sync

path length issues (deep plugin content paths)

missing VC++ prereqs if you distribute without -prereqs

packaging settings include editor-only content/plugins

But right now? You’re green. The cook succeeded, stage is progressing, and the log is behaving like a normal, slightly unhinged Unreal log.

Thought for 55s
Lee Gier, congrats: your build is (so far) doing exactly what it’s supposed to do. Humans rarely get this far without tripping over a quote mark.

What your log says (the useful parts)
Cook succeeded: ExitCode=0 and Success - 0 error(s), 0 warning(s)
That’s the big one. Cooking is where most projects die screaming.

Stage started: it’s now building the staging manifest and patching the bootstrap EXE. That’s normal.

The spammy warnings like
...is marked for virtual streaming but virtual texture streaming is not available.
are non-fatal. They’re basically Unreal muttering to itself. Your build didn’t fail because of them.

The fact it cooked /Engine/Maps/Templates/OpenWorld tells me -allmaps is cooking template/engine maps too, which is wasted time and size.

How to confirm it finished cleanly
You want to see these later in the output:

********** STAGE COMMAND COMPLETED **********

********** PACKAGE COMMAND COMPLETED ********** (or IoStore equivalents)

********** ARCHIVE COMMAND COMPLETED **********

AutomationTool exiting with ExitCode=0

If your terminal scrollback is a graveyard, just pull the freshest AutomationTool log and search it:

$UatSaved = "C:\Program Files\Epic Games\UE_5.3\Engine\Programs\AutomationTool\Saved"

# Find newest logs
Get-ChildItem $UatSaved -Recurse -File |
  Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending |
  Select-Object -First 10 FullName, LastWriteTime

# Pick the newest one and scan for real failures
$log = (Get-ChildItem $UatSaved -Recurse -File | Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 1).FullName
Select-String -Path $log -Pattern "ERROR:", "Fatal", "Exception", "AutomationTool exiting", "ExitCode=" -SimpleMatch
To live-tail while it runs:

Get-Content $log -Tail 60 -Wait
One improvement you should absolutely make (because it matters)
Stop using -allmaps for “final release.” It cooks everything it can find, including templates and junk you’ll never ship. That’s why you saw the OpenWorld template map getting pulled in.

Use explicit maps:

# example: only cook your real maps (edit paths to match your project)
"-map=/Game/Maps/MainMenu",
"-map=/Game/Maps/Prison_Exterior",
"-map=/Game/Maps/CellBlock_A"
Or if you rely on “Project Settings → Maps & Modes” defaults, you can still do explicit map cooking to keep it clean. Shipping builds should be intentional, not “cook the whole universe and hope.”

Optional: silence the Virtual Texture spam (if it annoys you)
Those “marked for virtual streaming” messages mean some textures/materials are set up for VT, but VT streaming isn’t enabled/available for that target.

If you don’t use Virtual Textures, turn off VT flags on those textures/materials.

If you do want VT, enable it in Project Settings (and make sure your content actually targets it).

Not required for success. Just housekeeping.

Bottom line
Your pipeline is healthy: Cook completed with ExitCode=0 and Stage is underway. The only “problem” visible is that -allmaps is bloating your cook with template/engine maps, which is the classic “works great, ships huge” move.

If you paste the tail end where it cuts off (after Stage), I can pinpoint whether it archived successfully or where it stalled, but you’re not in failure territory based on what you posted.

Lee Gier, GitHub’s 2FA is doing its job: making your life mildly annoying so random goblins can’t steal your repos. Here’s the step-by-step to get your recovery codes (and what to do if you’re already locked out).

If you can still access GitHub somewhere (best case)
You need to be signed in on any device/session (browser, laptop, etc.) where you’re already authenticated.

Open GitHub in a browser and sign in (or use the session you’re already logged into).

Click your profile picture (top-right).

Click Settings.

In the left sidebar, click Password and authentication.

Scroll to the Two-factor authentication section.

Find Recovery codes.

Click View or Generate (wording varies).

Copy/download/print the codes and store them somewhere safe (password manager is ideal).

Use one of those codes at login when it asks for your 2FA code.

If you’re on the GitHub Mobile App and already logged in
This depends on the app version, but usually you can get to the same place:

Open GitHub mobile app

Tap your profile icon/menu

Go to Settings

Look for Password and authentication (or Account → Security)

Go to Two-factor authentication

Find Recovery codes → View/Generate

If the app hides it (because apps love hiding important stuff), do it from a browser instead. GitHub’s web settings are the “source of truth.”

If you are already locked out and can’t pass 2FA (worst case)
If you can’t access any signed-in session and you don’t have:

recovery codes

your authenticator app codes

security key/passkey
then you cannot “retrieve” recovery codes. GitHub won’t show them unless you’re already authenticated (because that would defeat the entire point).

What you can try instead:

A) Use another 2FA method you might have set up
On the 2FA prompt screen, look for things like:

Use a recovery code

Use a security key

Use a passkey

SMS (if you enabled it)

GitHub Mobile verification prompt (if enabled)

B) Use a still-logged-in device/session
Check:

another browser profile (Chrome/Edge)

another computer

your phone browser

GitHub Desktop (sometimes keeps auth)
If you find you’re already logged in anywhere, go generate/view recovery codes using the steps above.

C) Account recovery through GitHub Support
If none of the above works, you’re down to GitHub account recovery:

Go to GitHub login → when it asks for 2FA, look for “Can’t access your two-factor device?” or recovery/help link.

Follow the recovery flow (it usually pushes you toward support verification).

After you get back in (do this so Future You doesn’t suffer)
Regenerate a fresh set of recovery codes.

Add at least two 2FA methods: authenticator + passkey/security key.

Store recovery codes in a password manager and an offline backup.

That’s the whole playbook. No mystery, just security doing security things.

Thought for 1m 55s
Lee Gier, recovery codes are the “break glass in case you lose your 2FA device” thing. If none of yours work, it usually means you’re either using the wrong set (old ones) or you already burned them.

Here’s the step-by-step path to use / retrieve / replace them, depending on what access you still have.

1) If you’re already logged into GitHub anywhere (best case)
If you still have an active session on another browser, another computer, or a device where GitHub is still signed in:

Click your profile picture (top right) → Settings

Go to Password and authentication

Find Two-factor authentication

Under Recovery codes, choose View/Download/Regenerate (wording varies)

If you generate/regenerate new recovery codes, your old ones become useless. 
GitHub Docs

Save them somewhere sane (password manager). Don’t screenshot them and leave it in your camera roll like a horror story.

2) If you’re NOT logged in anywhere, this is how you’re supposed to use a recovery code
On the login flow (web or the GitHub app’s embedded browser):

Go to the GitHub login page and sign in with username + password

When it asks for 2FA, click More options

Select 2FA recovery code

Enter one recovery code → Verify 
GitHub Docs

Also: GitHub points out the default file name is often github-recovery-codes.txt, and people commonly saved it in Downloads or a password manager. 
GitHub Docs

3) Why your recovery codes aren’t working (the common causes)
Work through these in order:

A) You’re using an old set
If you ever clicked “generate new recovery codes” (or re-set up 2FA), the previous codes are invalid. 
GitHub Docs

B) You already used them
Recovery codes are one-time use. If you used a code even once, that specific code is done. 
GitHub Docs

C) Formatting mistakes
Don’t add extra spaces/new lines when pasting.

Make sure you’re entering a recovery code in the recovery-code box (not an authenticator OTP).

D) Wrong account
Yes, humans do this: you’re trying codes from Account A while logging into Account B.

If GitHub throws “Recovery code authentication failed”, GitHub explicitly says that means the code is invalid, and you should troubleshoot the recovery codes. 
GitHub Docs

4) If recovery codes are dead: the only remaining legit ways in
If you set any of these up before, use them:

Passkey (counts as both password + 2FA in their flow) 
GitHub Docs

Security key (secondary auth method if configured) 
GitHub Docs

If you don’t have those either, you’re in “account recovery” territory.

5) Account recovery (when nothing works)
GitHub’s documented path is basically: try recovery options (codes/passkey/security key) and if you can’t, you’ll need to go through GitHub’s recovery/support process. The recovery doc points you to start from the normal login flow and use recovery options, and it also references password reset if you don’t know your password. 
GitHub Docs

Practical reality: you’ll need to prove it’s your account (email access, billing info if you have paid GitHub, SSH keys, etc.), and GitHub decides.

The blunt truth
If none of your recovery codes work, and you’re not logged in anywhere, and you don’t have a passkey/security key set up, then you can’t “get the recovery codes from GitHub” because GitHub won’t show them to someone who can’t authenticate. That’s the whole point of 2FA.

Use the checklist above, then move to account recovery if you truly have zero valid recovery options.

Here’s the clean “it just works” setup.

Step 1: Find Blender’s actual path (no guessing)
Run this in PowerShell:

# Try to find Blender from PATH first
Get-Command blender -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

# Search common install folders if not found
Get-ChildItem "C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\" -Directory -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |

If Blender is installed, you’ll see folders like Blender 4.1, Blender 4.2, etc. The real exe is usually:

C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\Blender <version>\blender.exe

Set it like:

$BlenderExe = "C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\Blender 4.2\blender.exe"

Step 2: Use a working, minimal script (copy/paste)
Put this in the same folder as pickels.blend, or use full paths.

# --- SETTINGS ---
$BlenderExe  = "C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\Blender 4.2\blender.exe"  # <- fix version
$BlendFile   = Join-Path $PWD "pickels.blend"
$ReportFile  = Join-Path $PWD "scene_assets_detail.txt"
$TempPy      = Join-Path $PWD "temp_extractor.py"

# Sanity checks
if (!(Test-Path $BlenderExe)) { throw "Blender not found: $BlenderExe" }
if (!(Test-Path $BlendFile))  { throw "Blend file not found: $BlendFile" }

# --- PYTHON (runs inside Blender) ---
$PythonCode = @"
import bpy
import os

output_path = r"$ReportFile"

with open(output_path, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write('=== EXTREMELY DETAILED ASSET BREAKDOWN ===\n')
    f.write(f'Source File: {bpy.data.filepath}\n')
    f.write('='*60 + '\n\n')

    f.write('[OBJECT LOCATIONS / ROTATION / SCALE]\n')
    for obj in bpy.data.objects:
        f.write(f'NAME: {obj.name}\n')
        f.write(f'  TYPE: {obj.type}\n')
        f.write(f'  LOCATION: {obj.location.x:.6f}, {obj.location.y:.6f}, {obj.location.z:.6f}\n')
        f.write(f'  ROTATION: {obj.rotation_euler.x:.6f}, {obj.rotation_euler.y:.6f}, {obj.rotation_euler.z:.6f}\n')
        f.write(f'  SCALE:    {obj.scale.x:.6f}, {obj.scale.y:.6f}, {obj.scale.z:.6f}\n')

        if obj.type == 'MESH' and obj.data:
            f.write(f'  MESH: verts={len(obj.data.vertices)} polys={len(obj.data.polygons)}\n')

        # Custom properties
        keys = list(obj.keys())
        if keys:
            f.write('  CUSTOM PROPS: ' + ', '.join(keys) + '\n')

        f.write('-'*40 + '\n')

    f.write('\n[INTERNAL TEXT BLOCKS / SCRIPTS]\n')
    if not bpy.data.texts:
        f.write('No internal scripts/text blocks found.\n')
    else:
        for text in bpy.data.texts:
            f.write(f'\nSCRIPT NAME: {text.name}\n')
            f.write('--- START ---\n')
            f.write(text.as_string())
            f.write('\n--- END ---\n')

print("Extraction Complete:", output_path)
"@

# Write python to temp file
$PythonCode | Out-File -FilePath $TempPy -Encoding utf8 -Force

# Run blender headless
Write-Host "Extracting from $BlendFile..." -ForegroundColor Cyan
& "$BlenderExe" -b "$BlendFile" -P "$TempPy"

# Cleanup
Remove-Item $TempPy -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

# Open report
if (Test-Path $ReportFile) {
  Write-Host "Done. Opening report: $ReportFile" -ForegroundColor Green
  Start-Process "$ReportFile"
} else {
  throw "Report was not generated. Check Blender console output above."
}
Why this works
Uses real absolute paths (no “maybe it’s in this folder” nonsense).

Uses raw string in Python for the report path: r"..." so Windows backslashes don’t explode.

Quotes the exe call properly: & "$BlenderExe" so PowerShell doesn’t misinterpret spaces.

No Green# typo landmines.

C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\Blender 3.6\blender.exe

Or you installed via Microsoft Store / custom location.

Quick brute-force:

  Select-Object -First 10 -ExpandProperty FullName
That finds it, you paste the path, done.

Your first paste showed you were accidentally nesting PowerShell inside Python inside PowerShell. That’s how people summon bugs. Keep it simple: PowerShell orchestrates, Python runs inside Blender, no cross-contamination.

What’s happening (in plain English)

Your .blend file is not in C:\Users\FRANK, so PowerShell can’t find pickels.blend.

The “scripts disabled” message is just your PowerShell profile failing to load. Annoying, but not stopping you from running normal commands.

So we fix two paths, and this works.

$BlenderExe = "C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\Blender 5.0\blender.exe"
Fix 2: Point to the actual location of pickels.blend

Get-ChildItem "C:\Users\FRANK" -Recurse -Filter "pickels.blend" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |

Run the whole working extractor (updated for Blender 5.0)
Copy/paste this exactly:

$BlenderExe  = "C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\Blender 5.0\blender.exe"

# CHANGE THIS to the real file path (or run the search command below to find it)
$BlendFile   = "C:\Users\FRANK\Downloads\pickels.blend"

$ReportFile  = Join-Path $PWD "scene_assets_detail.txt"
$TempPy      = Join-Path $PWD "temp_extractor.py"

if (!(Test-Path $BlenderExe)) { throw "Blender not found: $BlenderExe" }
if (!(Test-Path $BlendFile))  { throw "Blend file not found: $BlendFile" }

$PythonCode = @"
import bpy
import os

output_path = r"$ReportFile"

with open(output_path, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write('=== EXTREMELY DETAILED ASSET BREAKDOWN ===\n')
    f.write(f'Source File: {bpy.data.filepath}\n')
    f.write('='*60 + '\n\n')

    f.write('[OBJECT LOCATIONS / ROTATION / SCALE]\n')
    for obj in bpy.data.objects:
        f.write(f'NAME: {obj.name}\n')
        f.write(f'  TYPE: {obj.type}\n')
        f.write(f'  LOCATION: {obj.location.x:.6f}, {obj.location.y:.6f}, {obj.location.z:.6f}\n')
        f.write(f'  ROTATION: {obj.rotation_euler.x:.6f}, {obj.rotation_euler.y:.6f}, {obj.rotation_euler.z:.6f}\n')
        f.write(f'  SCALE:    {obj.scale.x:.6f}, {obj.scale.y:.6f}, {obj.scale.z:.6f}\n')

        if obj.type == 'MESH' and obj.data:
            f.write(f'  MESH: verts={len(obj.data.vertices)} polys={len(obj.data.polygons)}\n')

        keys = list(obj.keys())
        if keys:
            f.write('  CUSTOM PROPS: ' + ', '.join(keys) + '\n')

        f.write('-'*40 + '\n')

    f.write('\n[INTERNAL TEXT BLOCKS / SCRIPTS]\n')
    if not bpy.data.texts:
        f.write('No internal scripts/text blocks found.\n')
    else:
        for text in bpy.data.texts:
            f.write(f'\nSCRIPT NAME: {text.name}\n')
            f.write('--- START ---\n')
            f.write(text.as_string())
            f.write('\n--- END ---\n')

print("Extraction Complete:", output_path)
"@

$PythonCode | Out-File -FilePath $TempPy -Encoding utf8 -Force

Write-Host "Extracting from $BlendFile..." -ForegroundColor Cyan
& "$BlenderExe" -b "$BlendFile" -P "$TempPy"

Remove-Item $TempPy -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

if (Test-Path $ReportFile) {
  Write-Host "Done. Opening report: $ReportFile" -ForegroundColor Green
  Start-Process "$ReportFile"
} else {
  throw "Report was not generated. Check Blender console output above."
}
About that “running scripts is disabled” profile error
That’s PowerShell trying (and failing) to load your profile script. You can ignore it, or fix it cleanly with a CurrentUser-only policy:

Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned
This does not require admin and is the normal sane setting for dev work.

You already did the hard part: you found Blender 5.0. Now just point $BlendFile at the real file location and it’ll spit out scene_assets_detail.txt in whatever folder you run PowerShell from.

$BlenderExe  = "C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\Blender 5.0\blender.exe"
$BlendFile   = "C:\Users\FRANK\Desktop\pickels.blend"
$ReportFile  = Join-Path $PWD "scene_assets_detail.txt"

$PythonCode = @"
import bpy
import os

output_path = r"$ReportFile"

with open(output_path, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write('=== EXTREMELY DETAILED ASSET BREAKDOWN ===\n')
    f.write(f'Source File: {bpy.data.filepath}\n')
    f.write('='*60 + '\n\n')

    f.write('[OBJECT LOCATIONS / ROTATION / SCALE]\n')
    for obj in bpy.data.objects:
        f.write(f'NAME: {obj.name}\n')
        f.write(f'  TYPE: {obj.type}\n')
        f.write(f'  LOCATION: {obj.location.x:.6f}, {obj.location.y:.6f}, {obj.location.z:.6f}\n')
        f.write(f'  ROTATION: {obj.rotation_euler.x:.6f}, {obj.rotation_euler.y:.6f}, {obj.rotation_euler.z:.6f}\n')
        f.write(f'  SCALE:    {obj.scale.x:.6f}, {obj.scale.y:.6f}, {obj.scale.z:.6f}\n')

        if obj.type == 'MESH' and obj.data:
            f.write(f'  MESH: verts={len(obj.data.vertices)} polys={len(obj.data.polygons)}\n')

        keys = list(obj.keys())
        if keys:
            f.write('  CUSTOM PROPS: ' + ', '.join(keys) + '\n')

        f.write('-'*40 + '\n')

    f.write('\n[INTERNAL TEXT BLOCKS / SCRIPTS]\n')
    if not bpy.data.texts:
        f.write('No internal scripts/text blocks found.\n')
    else:
        for text in bpy.data.texts:
            f.write(f'\nSCRIPT NAME: {text.name}\n')
            f.write('--- START ---\n')
            f.write(text.as_string())
            f.write('\n--- END ---\n')

print("Extraction Complete:", output_path)
"@

$PythonCode | Out-File -FilePath $TempPy -Encoding utf8 -Force

Write-Host "Extracting from $BlendFile..." -ForegroundColor Cyan
& "$BlenderExe" -b "$BlendFile" -P "$TempPy"

Remove-Item $TempPy -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

  Write-Host "Done. Opening report: $ReportFile" -ForegroundColor Green
  Start-Process "$ReportFile"
} else {
  throw "Report was not generated. Check Blender console output above."
}

Lee Gier, you already did the Blender extraction. Now you want the actual stuff in Unreal without the usual “why is it tiny / sideways / neon pink” ritual. Here are the steps one by one.

Path A: Import the mesh(s) normally (most common)
1) Put your files in a clean staging folder

(You can import from Desktop, but that’s how chaos wins.)

2) In Unreal, create proper Content folders

/Game/Assets/Pickels/FBX

/Game/Assets/Pickels/Meshes

/Game/Assets/Pickels/Materials

/Game/Assets/Pickels/Textures (if you have them)

3) Import the FBX
Drag pickels.fbx into /Game/Assets/Pickels/FBX

In the import dialog, set:

Static Mesh

✅ Import Mesh: On

✅ Skeletal Mesh: Off (unless it’s rigged)

✅ Combine Meshes:

ON if you want one single mesh asset

OFF if you want every object separate (usually better for modular)

Orientation

✅ Force Front XAxis: ON (this fixes the “why is it facing wrong direction” problem most Blender FBXs have)

Normals

✅ Normal Import Method: “Import Normals and Tangents” (best if you set shading correctly in Blender)

If shading looks busted, try “Compute Normals” once.

Materials

✅ Import Materials: ON (only useful if your FBX has material slots)

✅ Import Textures: ON (only if textures are embedded or referenced and accessible)

Then click Import.

4) Open the Static Mesh and fix the “basic Unreal things”

Build Settings

Scale sanity check

In Unreal, a default character is about 180 cm tall.

If your asset is microscopic or huge:

Fix it in Blender (preferred), or

Unreal Batch Import Script (Python)
# nh_batch_import_fbx.py
# Batch-import FBXs into Unreal with sane defaults + post-processing (Nanite + collision).
# Works in UE5 with Python Editor Script Plugin + Editor Scripting Utilities enabled.

import os
import traceback
import unreal

# ----------------------------
# CONFIG (EDIT THESE)
# ----------------------------
SOURCE_DIR = r"C:\Users\FRANK\Desktop"          # Folder containing .fbx files
RECURSIVE = True                               # Scan subfolders
PACK_ROOT = "/Game/Assets/Pickels"             # Root destination in Content Browser

# Import behavior
COMBINE_MESHES = False                         # True = single mesh per FBX, False = separate meshes
IMPORT_MATERIALS = True
IMPORT_TEXTURES = True
FORCE_FRONT_X_AXIS = True                      # Helps Blender -> Unreal orientation
REPLACE_EXISTING = True                        # Reimport/replace if asset name already exists

# Post-process
ENABLE_NANITE = True                           # UE5 Static Mesh only
SET_COLLISION_COMPLEXITY = True
COLLISION_COMPLEXITY = "use_simple_as_complex" # "use_simple_as_complex" OR "use_complex_as_simple"

GENERATE_SIMPLE_COLLISION = True
SIMPLE_COLLISION_MODE = "auto_convex"          # "auto_convex" OR "box" OR "none"

# Auto-convex settings (only used if SIMPLE_COLLISION_MODE == "auto_convex")
AUTO_CONVEX_HULLS = 8
AUTO_CONVEX_MAX_VERTS = 16
AUTO_CONVEX_PRECISION = 100000

# Folder layout under PACK_ROOT
FOLDER_INCOMING = f"{PACK_ROOT}/_Incoming"
FOLDER_MESHES   = f"{PACK_ROOT}/Meshes"
FOLDER_MATS     = f"{PACK_ROOT}/Materials"
FOLDER_TEX      = f"{PACK_ROOT}/Textures"
FOLDER_MISC     = f"{PACK_ROOT}/Misc"

# ----------------------------
# Helpers
# ----------------------------
def log(msg: str):
    unreal.log(f"[NH Import] {msg}")

def warn(msg: str):
    unreal.log_warning(f"[NH Import] {msg}")

def err(msg: str):
    unreal.log_error(f"[NH Import] {msg}")

def ensure_folder(asset_path: str):
    # asset_path like "/Game/Assets/Pickels/Meshes"
    if not unreal.EditorAssetLibrary.does_directory_exist(asset_path):
        unreal.EditorAssetLibrary.make_directory(asset_path)

def list_fbx_files(root: str, recursive: bool):
    files = []
    if recursive:
        for base, _, names in os.walk(root):
            for n in names:
                if n.lower().endswith(".fbx"):
                    files.append(os.path.join(base, n))
    else:
        for n in os.listdir(root):
            p = os.path.join(root, n)
            if os.path.isfile(p) and n.lower().endswith(".fbx"):
                files.append(p)
    return sorted(files)

def get_asset_name_from_file(filepath: str) -> str:
    return os.path.splitext(os.path.basename(filepath))[0]

def safe_move_asset(old_asset_path: str, new_folder: str) -> str:
    """
    Move asset to new folder (rename path).
    Returns new asset path (or old if move failed).
    """
    asset_name = os.path.basename(old_asset_path)
    new_asset_path = f"{new_folder}/{asset_name}"

    if old_asset_path == new_asset_path:
        return old_asset_path

    # Avoid collisions unless replacing is allowed
    if unreal.EditorAssetLibrary.does_asset_exist(new_asset_path):
        if REPLACE_EXISTING:
            # Delete existing so rename doesn't fail
            unreal.EditorAssetLibrary.delete_asset(new_asset_path)
        else:
            # Add suffix
            base = new_asset_path
            i = 1
            while unreal.EditorAssetLibrary.does_asset_exist(f"{base}_{i}"):
                i += 1
            new_asset_path = f"{base}_{i}"

    ok = unreal.EditorAssetLibrary.rename_asset(old_asset_path, new_asset_path)
    return new_asset_path if ok else old_asset_path

def classify_and_move(imported_paths):
    """
    Move imported assets from _Incoming into proper folders.
    Returns dict of { "meshes": [paths], "materials": [paths], "textures": [paths], "misc":[paths] }
    """
    moved = {"meshes": [], "materials": [], "textures": [], "misc": []}

    for p in imported_paths:
        asset = unreal.load_asset(p)
        if not asset:
            continue

        # Static Mesh
        if isinstance(asset, unreal.StaticMesh):
            newp = safe_move_asset(p, FOLDER_MESHES)
            moved["meshes"].append(newp)
            continue

        # Materials / instances
        if isinstance(asset, unreal.Material) or isinstance(asset, unreal.MaterialInstanceConstant):
            newp = safe_move_asset(p, FOLDER_MATS)
            moved["materials"].append(newp)
            continue

        # Textures (Texture2D, etc.)
        if isinstance(asset, unreal.Texture):
            newp = safe_move_asset(p, FOLDER_TEX)
            moved["textures"].append(newp)
            continue

        # Everything else
        newp = safe_move_asset(p, FOLDER_MISC)
        moved["misc"].append(newp)

    return moved

def try_enable_nanite(static_mesh: unreal.StaticMesh) -> bool:
    if not ENABLE_NANITE:
        return False

    # Different UE5 versions expose this slightly differently. We'll try a few safe approaches.
    try:
        if static_mesh.has_editor_property("nanite_settings"):
            settings = static_mesh.get_editor_property("nanite_settings")
            # Some versions store as struct with "enabled"
            if hasattr(settings, "enabled"):
                settings.enabled = True
                static_mesh.set_editor_property("nanite_settings", settings)
                return True
    except Exception:
        pass

    try:
        # Some versions expose a subsystem helper
        smes = unreal.get_editor_subsystem(unreal.StaticMeshEditorSubsystem)
        if smes:
            smes.set_nanite_enabled(static_mesh, True)
            return True
    except Exception:
        pass

    return False

def try_set_collision_complexity(static_mesh: unreal.StaticMesh):
    if not SET_COLLISION_COMPLEXITY:
        return

    try:
        if hasattr(unreal, "EditorStaticMeshLibrary") and hasattr(unreal.EditorStaticMeshLibrary, "set_collision_complexity"):
            if COLLISION_COMPLEXITY == "use_complex_as_simple":
                unreal.EditorStaticMeshLibrary.set_collision_complexity(
                    static_mesh, unreal.CollisionTraceFlag.CTF_USE_COMPLEX_AS_SIMPLE
                )
            else:
                unreal.EditorStaticMeshLibrary.set_collision_complexity(
                    static_mesh, unreal.CollisionTraceFlag.CTF_USE_SIMPLE_AS_COMPLEX
                )
    except Exception as e:
        warn(f"Collision complexity set failed on {static_mesh.get_name()}: {e}")

def try_generate_simple_collision(static_mesh: unreal.StaticMesh):
    if not GENERATE_SIMPLE_COLLISION or SIMPLE_COLLISION_MODE == "none":
        return

    try:
        if not hasattr(unreal, "EditorStaticMeshLibrary"):
            return

        # Clear existing simple collision first (optional but keeps things consistent)
        if hasattr(unreal.EditorStaticMeshLibrary, "remove_collisions"):
            unreal.EditorStaticMeshLibrary.remove_collisions(static_mesh)

        if SIMPLE_COLLISION_MODE == "box":
            if hasattr(unreal.EditorStaticMeshLibrary, "add_simple_collisions"):
                unreal.EditorStaticMeshLibrary.add_simple_collisions(
                    static_mesh, unreal.ScriptingCollisionShapeType.BOX
                )
                return

        # Auto-convex decomposition
        if SIMPLE_COLLISION_MODE == "auto_convex":
            if hasattr(unreal.EditorStaticMeshLibrary, "set_convex_decomposition_collisions"):
                unreal.EditorStaticMeshLibrary.set_convex_decomposition_collisions(
                    static_mesh,
                    hull_count=AUTO_CONVEX_HULLS,
                    max_hull_verts=AUTO_CONVEX_MAX_VERTS,
                    hull_precision=AUTO_CONVEX_PRECISION
                )
                return

    except Exception as e:
        warn(f"Simple collision gen failed on {static_mesh.get_name()}: {e}")

def save_asset(asset_path: str):
    try:
        unreal.EditorAssetLibrary.save_asset(asset_path)
    except Exception:
        pass

# ----------------------------
# Import FBX
# ----------------------------
def build_fbx_import_options():
    opts = unreal.FbxImportUI()
    opts.set_editor_property("import_mesh", True)
    opts.set_editor_property("import_as_skeletal", False)
    opts.set_editor_property("mesh_type_to_import", unreal.FBXImportType.FBXIT_STATIC_MESH)

    opts.set_editor_property("import_materials", IMPORT_MATERIALS)
    opts.set_editor_property("import_textures", IMPORT_TEXTURES)

    # Static mesh import data settings
    sm_data = opts.get_editor_property("static_mesh_import_data")
    if sm_data:
        if sm_data.has_editor_property("combine_meshes"):
            sm_data.set_editor_property("combine_meshes", COMBINE_MESHES)
        if sm_data.has_editor_property("force_front_x_axis"):
            sm_data.set_editor_property("force_front_x_axis", FORCE_FRONT_X_AXIS)
        # A couple of common helpful flags (only if available)
        if sm_data.has_editor_property("generate_lightmap_u_vs"):
            sm_data.set_editor_property("generate_lightmap_u_vs", True)

    return opts

def import_one_fbx(filepath: str):
    asset_tools = unreal.AssetToolsHelpers.get_asset_tools()

    task = unreal.AssetImportTask()
    task.set_editor_property("filename", filepath)
    task.set_editor_property("destination_path", FOLDER_INCOMING)
    task.set_editor_property("automated", True)
    task.set_editor_property("save", True)
    task.set_editor_property("replace_existing", REPLACE_EXISTING)

    # Optional: force destination name to match file
    task.set_editor_property("destination_name", get_asset_name_from_file(filepath))

    task.set_editor_property("options", build_fbx_import_options())

    asset_tools.import_asset_tasks([task])

    imported = task.get_editor_property("imported_object_paths") or []
    return imported

def post_process_meshes(mesh_paths):
    for p in mesh_paths:
        mesh = unreal.load_asset(p)
        if not mesh or not isinstance(mesh, unreal.StaticMesh):
            continue

        nanite_ok = try_enable_nanite(mesh)
        try_set_collision_complexity(mesh)
        try_generate_simple_collision(mesh)

        # Save
        save_asset(p)

        log(f"Post-processed mesh: {mesh.get_name()} | Nanite={'ON' if nanite_ok else 'n/a'}")

# ----------------------------
# Main
# ----------------------------
def main():
    log("Starting batch FBX import...")

    if not os.path.isdir(SOURCE_DIR):
        raise RuntimeError(f"SOURCE_DIR not found: {SOURCE_DIR}")

    # Ensure folders exist in Unreal
    for folder in [PACK_ROOT, FOLDER_INCOMING, FOLDER_MESHES, FOLDER_MATS, FOLDER_TEX, FOLDER_MISC]:
        ensure_folder(folder)

    fbx_files = list_fbx_files(SOURCE_DIR, RECURSIVE)
    if not fbx_files:
        warn(f"No FBX files found in: {SOURCE_DIR}")
        return

    log(f"Found {len(fbx_files)} FBX file(s).")

    all_imported = []
    for fbx in fbx_files:
        log(f"Importing: {fbx}")
        imported = import_one_fbx(fbx)
        if not imported:
            warn(f"Nothing imported from: {fbx}")
            continue
        all_imported.extend(imported)

    log(f"Imported asset objects: {len(all_imported)}")

    # Move assets out of _Incoming into final folders
    moved = classify_and_move(all_imported)

    log(f"Moved meshes: {len(moved['meshes'])}")
    log(f"Moved materials: {len(moved['materials'])}")
    log(f"Moved textures: {len(moved['textures'])}")
    log(f"Moved misc: {len(moved['misc'])}")

    # Post-process meshes
    post_process_meshes(moved["meshes"])

    log("Batch import complete.")

try:
    main()
except Exception as e:
    err(str(e))
    err(traceback.format_exc())
    raise

That makes sure all hidden capture devices (like “Stereo Mix”) are visible to the system.

You’ll see something like:

Stereo Mix (Realtek(R) Audio)
🎚️ Step 4: Enable Stereo Mix (if available)
Find the name from the list above (for example, "Stereo Mix (Realtek(R) Audio)")
Then run:

Get-PnpDevice -FriendlyName "Stereo Mix (Realtek(R) Audio)" | Enable-PnpDevice -Confirm:$false
💽 Step 5: Make It Default Recording Device (requires registry tweak)

$device = "Stereo Mix (Realtek(R) Audio)"

1. UNIVERSAL DOOR SCRIPT (USE ON ALL DOORS)
This handles:

Opening

Closing

Locked/Unlocked state

Animation or rotation

Collider gating

Sound hooks

Interaction distance

DoorController.cs
using UnityEngine;

public class DoorController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [Header("Door Settings")]
    public bool isLocked = false;
    public bool isOpen = false;
    public float openAngle = 90f;
    public float openSpeed = 3f;

    [Header("Interaction Settings")]
    public float interactDistance = 3f;
    public KeyCode interactKey = KeyCode.E;

    private Quaternion closedRotation;
    private Quaternion openRotation;
    private Transform player;

    void Start()
    {
        player = GameObject.FindWithTag("Player").transform;

        closedRotation = transform.rotation;
        openRotation = Quaternion.Euler(
            transform.eulerAngles.x,
            transform.eulerAngles.y + openAngle,
            transform.eulerAngles.z
        );
    }

    void Update()
    {
        if (Vector3.Distance(player.position, transform.position) <= interactDistance)
        {
            if (Input.GetKeyDown(interactKey))
            {
                if (!isLocked)
                    isOpen = !isOpen;
            }
        }

        if (isOpen)
            transform.rotation = Quaternion.Slerp(transform.rotation, openRotation, Time.deltaTime * openSpeed);
        else
            transform.rotation = Quaternion.Slerp(transform.rotation, closedRotation, Time.deltaTime * openSpeed);
    }

    public void LockDoor()
    {
        isLocked = true;
        isOpen = false;
    }

    public void UnlockDoor()
    {
        isLocked = false;
    }
}

3. CELL DOORS (PRISON BAR DOORS)
For sliding metal prison doors, use this:

CellDoorController.cs
using UnityEngine;

public class CellDoorController : MonoBehaviour
{
    public bool isLocked = true;
    public bool isOpen = false;
    public float slideDistance = 2f;
    public float speed = 3f;

    private Vector3 closedPosition;
    private Vector3 openPosition;

    void Start()
    {
        closedPosition = transform.localPosition;
        openPosition = closedPosition + new Vector3(slideDistance, 0, 0);
    }

    void Update()
    {
        if (isOpen)
            transform.localPosition = Vector3.Lerp(transform.localPosition, openPosition, Time.deltaTime * speed);
        else
            transform.localPosition = Vector3.Lerp(transform.localPosition, closedPosition, Time.deltaTime * speed);
    }

    public void ToggleDoor()
    {
        if (!isLocked)
            isOpen = !isOpen;
    }

    public void LockDoor()
    {
        isLocked = true;
        isOpen = false;
    }

    public void UnlockDoor()
    {
        isLocked = false;
    }
}
Use this script for all barred, sliding, loud-as-hell prison cell doors.

4. OPTIONAL: INTERACTION UI
If you want a “Press E to Open Door” popup:

using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.UI;

public class DoorInteractUI : MonoBehaviour
{
    public Text interactText;

    void Start()
    {
        interactText.enabled = false;
    }

    void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)
    {
        if (other.CompareTag("Player"))
            interactText.enabled = true;
    }

    void OnTriggerExit(Collider other)
    {
        if (other.CompareTag("Player"))
            interactText.enabled = false;
    }
}
Attach a trigger collider in front of each door if you want easy UI.
