Commit and Push to GitHub:

git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit of Nightshade website"
git push origin main
Step 3: Set Up GitHub Actions for Continuous Deployment
Now, let’s automate the deployment process using GitHub Actions.

GitHub Actions Workflow for Netlify Deployment
Create a GitHub Action Workflow File:
In your repository, create the following folder structure and file:

.github/
  workflows/
    deploy.yml
Configure GitHub Actions:
In the deploy.yml file, add the following YAML code:

name: Deploy Website to Netlify

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v2

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v2
        with:
          node-version: '16'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm install

      - name: Deploy to Netlify
        uses: netlify/actions/cli-action@v1
        with:
          site_id: ${{ secrets.NETLIFY_SITE_ID }}
          access_token: ${{ secrets.NETLIFY_ACCESS_TOKEN }}
NETLIFY_SITE_ID: You can find this in your Netlify site settings.

NETLIFY_ACCESS_TOKEN: You can generate a personal access token in your Netlify Account Settings.

GitHub Actions Workflow for Vercel Deployment
If you prefer Vercel for deployment, you can use the following workflow.

Configure GitHub Actions for Vercel:
In the deploy.yml file, add the following YAML code:

name: Deploy Website to Vercel

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  pull_request:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v2

      - name: Set up Vercel
        uses: amondnet/vercel-action@v20
        with:
          vercel-token: ${{ secrets.VERCEL_TOKEN }}
          vercel-org-id: ${{ secrets.VERCEL_ORG_ID }}
          vercel-project-id: ${{ secrets.VERCEL_PROJECT_ID }}
          vercel-args: '--prod'
VERCEL_TOKEN: You can generate a personal access token in your Vercel Account Settings.

VERCEL_ORG_ID & VERCEL_PROJECT_ID: You can find these in your Vercel project settings.

Step 4: Add Secrets to GitHub
Go to your GitHub repository → Settings → Secrets.

Add the following secrets for Netlify or Vercel:

For Netlify:

NETLIFY_SITE_ID

NETLIFY_ACCESS_TOKEN

For Vercel:

VERCEL_TOKEN

VERCEL_ORG_ID

VERCEL_PROJECT_ID

Step 5: Push to GitHub
Commit the Action Workflow:
Add and commit the .github/workflows/deploy.yml file:

git add .github/workflows/deploy.yml
git commit -m "Set up GitHub Actions for Netlify/Vercel deployment"
git push origin main
Trigger the Workflow:
Once the files are pushed to GitHub, the GitHub Action will automatically trigger and deploy your website to Netlify or Vercel.

Step 6: Finalize the Website
Once the deployment is successful, you will receive a link to your live site. You can also connect a custom domain to either Netlify or Vercel.

Summary
With the above automation setup, every time you push to the main branch of your GitHub repository, your website will automatically:

Build using GitHub Actions.

Deploy to Netlify or Vercel.

Automatically be updated, and all links, GitHub profiles, and plugins will be ready to go.

It looks like you're working with npm and encountering an error because the package.json file is missing or not found. This file is essential for managing your Node.js project dependencies and scripts. If you don't have a package.json file in your project directory, you can generate one using the following command:

npm init
This will walk you through creating the file with necessary details like project name, version, description, entry point (usually index.js), etc. If you just need a basic package.json and don't want to go through the prompts, you can use:

npm init -y
This will generate a default package.json file. You can later edit this file to add dependencies or modify scripts.

Once you have the package.json in place, running npm install will work without errors, as it will recognize the file and manage your dependencies accordingly.

    "name": "Nyghtshade Assistant",
    "blender": (3, 0, 0),
    "category": "AI"
}

import bpy

class NyghtshadePanel(bpy.types.Panel):
    bl_label = "Nyghtshade"
    bl_idname = "NYGHTSHADE_PT_main"
    bl_space_type = 'VIEW_3D'

    def draw(self, context):
        layout = self.layout
        layout.operator("nyghtshade.ask_ai")

class AskAI(bpy.types.Operator):
    bl_idname = "nyghtshade.ask_ai"
    bl_label = "Ask AI"

    def execute(self, context):
        # send scene mesh + prompt
        return {'FINISHED'}

def register():
    bpy.utils.register_class(NyghtshadePanel)
    bpy.utils.register_class(AskAI)

def unregister():
    bpy.utils.unregister_class(NyghtshadePanel)

🗣️ Voice Command Grammar — Expanded (Intent Map)
Here’s a more structured grammar resembling SRGS (simplified):

<grammar version="1.0">
  <rule id="root">
    <one-of>
      <item> place <asset> (around | near | inside) <location> </item>
      <item> generate <script_type> for <purpose> </item>
      <item> find <asset_type> </item>
      <item> translate to <language> </item>
      <item> set theme to <theme> </item>
    </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="asset">
    <one-of> crate crates torch torches tree trees npc enemies </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="location">
    <one-of> castle keep forest path road </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="script_type">
    <one-of> C# Python blueprint behavior </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="language">
    <one-of> English Spanish Chinese French </one-of>
  </rule>

</grammar>
This gives a production grammar that NLP models can map to command intents.

# THE NYGHTSHADE DEVICE - FULL SPECS PACKAGE

## ✅ Contextual System Enhancements

### 1. Project Context Awareness
- Parse scene hierarchies and object references
- Understand prefab nesting and connections
- Lighting & physics awareness (e.g., global vs local light sources)
- Nav mesh analysis for AI pathing validation
- Animation FSM/state machine parsing
- Material/shader type classification

### 2. Versioning & Undo/Redo
- AI actions stored in undo buffer
- Git‑based diffs with commit previews
- Backup checkpoints after every generation

### 3. AI Safety & Rollback
- Pre-apply previews (visual + textual diff)
- Rollback commands or full scenes
- Confirmation steps for destructive edits

### 4. Automated Testing & Validation
- Auto‑generate unit tests
- Validate nav meshes
- Lint code for style/performance issues
- AI test bots (simulate player movement for coverage)

### 5. Performance Reporting
- Scene stats: draw calls, shader counts, object count
- Memory predictions for textures, animations, audio
- Lighting budget + bake warnings

### 6. Live Collaboration
- Shared AI sessions (like VS Live Share)
- Collaborative annotations
- AI change history for each user

### 7. Personal Pipeline Extensions
- Users define custom AI macros (DSL or YAML)
- Behavior injection into scenes
- Macros can be shared/exported

# nyghtshade/main.py

import sys


def show_help():
    print("""
    🧠 Nyghtshade CLI
    --------------------------
    Commands:
      scan         → Scan scene/project folder
      place        → Place assets using scene analysis
      gen-script   → Generate code/script via AI
      config       → Configure settings
      help         → Show this help menu
    """)


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        show_help()
        return

    command = sys.argv[1].lower()

    if command == "scan":
        print("🔍 Scanning scene... (placeholder logic)")
    elif command == "place":
        print("📦 Placing assets... (placeholder layout logic)")
    elif command == "gen-script":
        print("🧠 Generating code using AI... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "config":
        print("⚙️  Configuration module not yet implemented")
    else:
        show_help()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

import sys

def show_help():
    print("""
    🧠 Nyghtshade CLI
    --------------------------
    Commands:
      scan         → Scan scene/project folder
      place        → Place assets using scene analysis
      gen-script   → Generate code/script via AI
      config       → Configure settings
      help         → Show this help menu
    """)

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        show_help()
        return

    command = sys.argv[1].lower()

    if command == "scan":
        print("🔍 Scanning scene... (placeholder logic)")
    elif command == "place":
        print("📦 Placing assets... (placeholder layout logic)")
    elif command == "gen-script":
        print("🧠 Generating code using AI... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "config":
        print("⚙️  Configuration module not yet implemented")
    else:
        show_help()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

📌 cli/main.py
import sys

def show_help():
    print("""
    🧠 Nyghtshade CLI
    --------------------------
    Commands:
      scan         → Scan scene/project folder
      place        → Place assets using scene analysis
      gen-script   → Generate code/script via AI
      config       → Configure settings
      help         → Show this menu
    """)

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        show_help()
        return

    command = sys.argv[1].lower()

    if command == "scan":
        print("🔍 Scanning scene... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "place":
        print("📦 Placing assets... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "gen-script":
        print("🧠 Generating code... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "config":
        print("⚙️  Configuration module not implemented")
    else:
        show_help()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

📄 grammar.srgs (Extended)
<grammar version="1.0" xml:lang="en-US">
  <rule id="root" scope="public">
    <one-of>
      <item>place <asset> (around | in | near) <location></item>
      <item>generate <script_type> for <purpose></item>
      <item>scan project assets</item>
      <item>optimize scene performance</item>
      <item>translate to <language></item>
    </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="asset">
    <one-of>crate crates tree trees npc character enemy item weapon</one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="location">
    <one-of>forest village castle base road path</one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="script_type">
    <one-of>C# C++ python blueprint behavior shader</one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="purpose">
    <one-of>AI patrol attack move idle</one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="language">
    <one-of>English Spanish Chinese French</one-of>
  </rule>
</grammar>

import bpy

class NyghtshadePanel(bpy.types.Panel):
    bl_label = "Nyghtshade"
    bl_idname = "NYGHTSHADE_PT_main"
    bl_space_type = 'VIEW_3D'

    def draw(self, context):
        layout = self.layout
        layout.operator("nyghtshade.ask_ai")

class AskAI(bpy.types.Operator):
    bl_idname = "nyghtshade.ask_ai"
    bl_label = "Ask AI"

    def execute(self, context):
        # send scene mesh + prompt
        return {'FINISHED'}

def register():
    bpy.utils.register_class(NyghtshadePanel)
    bpy.utils.register_class(AskAI)

def unregister():
    bpy.utils.unregister_class(NyghtshadePanel)

🗣️ Voice Command Grammar — Expanded (Intent Map)
Here’s a more structured grammar resembling SRGS (simplified):

<grammar version="1.0">
  <rule id="root">
    <one-of>
      <item> place <asset> (around | near | inside) <location> </item>
      <item> generate <script_type> for <purpose> </item>
      <item> find <asset_type> </item>
      <item> translate to <language> </item>
      <item> set theme to <theme> </item>
    </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="asset">
    <one-of> crate crates torch torches tree trees npc enemies </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="location">
    <one-of> castle keep forest path road </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="script_type">
    <one-of> C# Python blueprint behavior </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="language">
    <one-of> English Spanish Chinese French </one-of>
  </rule>

</grammar>
This gives a production grammar that NLP models can map to command intents.

# THE NYGHTSHADE DEVICE - FULL SPECS PACKAGE

## ✅ Contextual System Enhancements

### 1. Project Context Awareness
- Parse scene hierarchies and object references
- Understand prefab nesting and connections
- Lighting & physics awareness (e.g., global vs local light sources)
- Nav mesh analysis for AI pathing validation
- Animation FSM/state machine parsing
- Material/shader type classification

### 2. Versioning & Undo/Redo
- AI actions stored in undo buffer
- Git‑based diffs with commit previews
- Backup checkpoints after every generation

### 3. AI Safety & Rollback
- Pre-apply previews (visual + textual diff)
- Rollback commands or full scenes
- Confirmation steps for destructive edits

### 4. Automated Testing & Validation
- Auto‑generate unit tests
- Validate nav meshes
- Lint code for style/performance issues
- AI test bots (simulate player movement for coverage)

### 5. Performance Reporting
- Scene stats: draw calls, shader counts, object count
- Memory predictions for textures, animations, audio
- Lighting budget + bake warnings

### 6. Live Collaboration
- Shared AI sessions (like VS Live Share)
- Collaborative annotations
- AI change history for each user

### 7. Personal Pipeline Extensions
- Users define custom AI macros (DSL or YAML)
- Behavior injection into scenes
- Macros can be shared/exported

📌 cli/main.py
import sys

def show_help():
    print("""
    🧠 Nyghtshade CLI
    --------------------------
    Commands:
      scan         → Scan scene/project folder
      place        → Place assets using scene analysis
      gen-script   → Generate code/script via AI
      config       → Configure settings
      help         → Show this menu
    """)

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        show_help()
        return

    command = sys.argv[1].lower()

    if command == "scan":
        print("🔍 Scanning scene... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "place":
        print("📦 Placing assets... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "gen-script":
        print("🧠 Generating code... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "config":
        print("⚙️  Configuration module not implemented")
    else:
        show_help()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

bl_info = {
    "name": "Nyghtshade Assistant",
    "blender": (3, 0, 0),
    "category": "AI"
}

import bpy

class NyghtshadePanel(bpy.types.Panel):
    bl_label = "Nyghtshade"
    bl_idname = "NYGHTSHADE_PT_main"
    bl_space_type = 'VIEW_3D'

    def draw(self, context):
        layout = self.layout
        layout.operator("nyghtshade.ask_ai")

class AskAI(bpy.types.Operator):
    bl_idname = "nyghtshade.ask_ai"
    bl_label = "Ask AI"

    def execute(self, context):
        # send scene mesh + prompt
        return {'FINISHED'}

def register():
    bpy.utils.register_class(NyghtshadePanel)
    bpy.utils.register_class(AskAI)

def unregister():
    bpy.utils.unregister_class(NyghtshadePanel)

  <rule id="root">
    <one-of>
      <item> place <asset> (around | near | inside) <location> </item>
      <item> generate <script_type> for <purpose> </item>
      <item> find <asset_type> </item>
      <item> translate to <language> </item>
      <item> set theme to <theme> </item>
    </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="asset">
    <one-of> crate crates torch torches tree trees npc enemies </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="location">
    <one-of> castle keep forest path road </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="script_type">
    <one-of> C# Python blueprint behavior </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="language">
    <one-of> English Spanish Chinese French </one-of>
  </rule>

</grammar>
This gives a production grammar that NLP models can map to command intents.

# nyghtshade/main.py

import sys


def show_help():
    print("""
    🧠 Nyghtshade CLI
    --------------------------
    Commands:
      scan         → Scan scene/project folder
      place        → Place assets using scene analysis
      gen-script   → Generate code/script via AI
      config       → Configure settings
      help         → Show this help menu
    """)


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        show_help()
        return

    command = sys.argv[1].lower()

    if command == "scan":
        print("🔍 Scanning scene... (placeholder logic)")
    elif command == "place":
        print("📦 Placing assets... (placeholder layout logic)")
    elif command == "gen-script":
        print("🧠 Generating code using AI... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "config":
        print("⚙️  Configuration module not yet implemented")
    else:
        show_help()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

🧪 cli/main.py
import sys

def show_help():
    print("""
    🧠 Nyghtshade CLI
    --------------------------
    Commands:
      scan         → Scan scene/project folder
      place        → Place assets using scene analysis
      gen-script   → Generate code/script via AI
      config       → Configure settings
      help         → Show this help menu
    """)

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        show_help()
        return

    command = sys.argv[1].lower()

    if command == "scan":
        print("🔍 Scanning scene... (placeholder logic)")
    elif command == "place":
        print("📦 Placing assets... (placeholder layout logic)")
    elif command == "gen-script":
        print("🧠 Generating code using AI... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "config":
        print("⚙️  Configuration module not yet implemented")
    else:
        show_help()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

📌 cli/main.py
import sys

def show_help():
    print("""
    🧠 Nyghtshade CLI
    --------------------------
    Commands:
      scan         → Scan scene/project folder
      place        → Place assets using scene analysis
      gen-script   → Generate code/script via AI
      config       → Configure settings
      help         → Show this menu
    """)

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        show_help()
        return

    command = sys.argv[1].lower()

    if command == "scan":
        print("🔍 Scanning scene... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "place":
        print("📦 Placing assets... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "gen-script":
        print("🧠 Generating code... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "config":
        print("⚙️  Configuration module not implemented")
    else:
        show_help()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

🧩 CORE 1 — CLI (WORKING)
cli/main.py
import sys
from scan import scan_project
from place import place_assets
from gen import generate_code

def help():
    print("""
NYGHTSHADE DEVICE CLI
--------------------
scan <path>              Scan project assets
place <asset> <count>    Place assets intelligently
gen <lang> <task>        Generate code or logic
""")

if len(sys.argv) < 2:
    help()
    sys.exit(0)

cmd = sys.argv[1]

if cmd == "scan":
    scan_project(sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else ".")
elif cmd == "place":
    place_assets(sys.argv[2], int(sys.argv[3]))
elif cmd == "gen":
    generate_code(sys.argv[2], " ".join(sys.argv[3:]))
else:
    help()
cli/scan.py
import os
import json

def scan_project(path):
    assets = []
    for root, _, files in os.walk(path):
        for f in files:
            if f.endswith((".fbx",".obj",".png",".wav",".cs",".cpp",".py")):
                assets.append(os.path.join(root, f))

    with open("data/assets.json","w") as out:
        json.dump(assets, out, indent=2)

    print(f"[✓] Scanned {len(assets)} assets")
🧠 CORE 2 — SCENE ANALYSIS + PLACEMENT (REAL LOGIC)
engine/layout_engine.py
import math

def grid_layout(area_width, area_depth, count, spacing=2.0):
    positions = []
    cols = int(math.sqrt(count))
    rows = math.ceil(count / cols)

    for i in range(count):
        x = (i % cols) * spacing
        z = (i // cols) * spacing
        positions.append({
            "x": x,
            "y": 0,
            "z": z
        })
    return positions
cli/place.py
from engine.layout_engine import grid_layout
import json

def place_assets(asset, count):
    layout = grid_layout(50, 50, count)
    output = {
        "asset": asset,
        "placements": layout
    }

    with open("data/placements.json","w") as f:
        json.dump(output, f, indent=2)

    print(f"[✓] Placed {count} {asset}")
This already produces Unity / Unreal compatible transform data.

    "name": "Nyghtshade Assistant",
    "blender": (3, 0, 0),
    "category": "AI"
}

import bpy

class NyghtshadePanel(bpy.types.Panel):
    bl_label = "Nyghtshade"
    bl_idname = "NYGHTSHADE_PT_main"
    bl_space_type = 'VIEW_3D'

    def draw(self, context):
        layout = self.layout
        layout.operator("nyghtshade.ask_ai")

class AskAI(bpy.types.Operator):
    bl_idname = "nyghtshade.ask_ai"
    bl_label = "Ask AI"

    def execute(self, context):
        # send scene mesh + prompt
        return {'FINISHED'}

def register():
    bpy.utils.register_class(NyghtshadePanel)
    bpy.utils.register_class(AskAI)

def unregister():
    bpy.utils.unregister_class(NyghtshadePanel)

🗣️ Voice Command Grammar — Expanded (Intent Map)
Here’s a more structured grammar resembling SRGS (simplified):

<grammar version="1.0">
  <rule id="root">
    <one-of>
      <item> place <asset> (around | near | inside) <location> </item>
      <item> generate <script_type> for <purpose> </item>
      <item> find <asset_type> </item>
      <item> translate to <language> </item>
      <item> set theme to <theme> </item>
    </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="asset">
    <one-of> crate crates torch torches tree trees npc enemies </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="location">
    <one-of> castle keep forest path road </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="script_type">
    <one-of> C# Python blueprint behavior </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="language">
    <one-of> English Spanish Chinese French </one-of>
  </rule>

</grammar>
This gives a production grammar that NLP models can map to command intents.

# nyghtshade/main.py

import sys


def show_help():
    print("""
    🧠 Nyghtshade CLI
    --------------------------
    Commands:
      scan         → Scan scene/project folder
      place        → Place assets using scene analysis
      gen-script   → Generate code/script via AI
      config       → Configure settings
      help         → Show this help menu
    """)


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        show_help()
        return

    command = sys.argv[1].lower()

    if command == "scan":
        print("🔍 Scanning scene... (placeholder logic)")
    elif command == "place":
        print("📦 Placing assets... (placeholder layout logic)")
    elif command == "gen-script":
        print("🧠 Generating code using AI... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "config":
        print("⚙️  Configuration module not yet implemented")
    else:
        show_help()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

🧪 cli/main.py
import sys

def show_help():
    print("""
    🧠 Nyghtshade CLI
    --------------------------
    Commands:
      scan         → Scan scene/project folder
      place        → Place assets using scene analysis
      gen-script   → Generate code/script via AI
      config       → Configure settings
      help         → Show this help menu
    """)

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        show_help()
        return

    command = sys.argv[1].lower()

    if command == "scan":
        print("🔍 Scanning scene... (placeholder logic)")
    elif command == "place":
        print("📦 Placing assets... (placeholder layout logic)")
    elif command == "gen-script":
        print("🧠 Generating code using AI... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "config":
        print("⚙️  Configuration module not yet implemented")
    else:
        show_help()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

📌 cli/main.py
import sys

def show_help():
    print("""
    🧠 Nyghtshade CLI
    --------------------------
    Commands:
      scan         → Scan scene/project folder
      place        → Place assets using scene analysis
      gen-script   → Generate code/script via AI
      config       → Configure settings
      help         → Show this menu
    """)

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        show_help()
        return

    command = sys.argv[1].lower()

    if command == "scan":
        print("🔍 Scanning scene... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "place":
        print("📦 Placing assets... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "gen-script":
        print("🧠 Generating code... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "config":
        print("⚙️  Configuration module not implemented")
    else:
        show_help()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

### 📌 **voice/grammar.srgs**
xml
<grammar version="1.0">
  <rule id="root">
    <one-of>
      <item>place <asset> in <location></item>
      <item>generate <script_type> for <purpose></item>
    </one-of>
  </rule>
</grammar>
📌 voice/commands.json
{
  "commands": [
    {"intent": "place_asset", "pattern": "place {asset} in {location}"},
    {"intent": "generate_code", "pattern": "generate {script_type} for {purpose}"}
  ]
}

Key Concepts Explained:

Core Services take natural language + voice → interpret it → dispatch to the right tool.

Scene Analyzer reads a scene’s mesh graph and spits out actionable data (surface normals, bounds, slopes, etc.).

Asset Discovery crawls local and remote repos, labels assets, and catalogs them.

Plugin Bridge lets the assistant “live inside” external tools (Unity, Unreal, Blender, VS Code).

🌀 Blender Addon (Python)
bl_info = {
    "name": "Nyghtshade Assistant",
    "blender": (3, 0, 0),
    "category": "AI"
}

import bpy

class NyghtshadePanel(bpy.types.Panel):
    bl_label = "Nyghtshade"
    bl_idname = "NYGHTSHADE_PT_main"
    bl_space_type = 'VIEW_3D'

    def draw(self, context):
        layout = self.layout
        layout.operator("nyghtshade.ask_ai")

class AskAI(bpy.types.Operator):
    bl_idname = "nyghtshade.ask_ai"
    bl_label = "Ask AI"

    def execute(self, context):
        # send scene mesh + prompt
        return {'FINISHED'}

def register():
    bpy.utils.register_class(NyghtshadePanel)
    bpy.utils.register_class(AskAI)

def unregister():
    bpy.utils.unregister_class(NyghtshadePanel)

🗣️ Voice Command Grammar — Expanded (Intent Map)
Here’s a more structured grammar resembling SRGS (simplified):

<grammar version="1.0">
  <rule id="root">
    <one-of>
      <item> place <asset> (around | near | inside) <location> </item>
      <item> generate <script_type> for <purpose> </item>
      <item> find <asset_type> </item>
      <item> translate to <language> </item>
      <item> set theme to <theme> </item>
    </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="asset">
    <one-of> crate crates torch torches tree trees npc enemies </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="location">
    <one-of> castle keep forest path road </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="script_type">
    <one-of> C# Python blueprint behavior </one-of>
  </rule>

  <rule id="language">
    <one-of> English Spanish Chinese French </one-of>
  </rule>

</grammar>
This gives a production grammar that NLP models can map to command intents.

<grammar version="1.0"> <rule id="root"> <one-of> <item> place <asset> (around | near | inside) <location> </item> <item> generate <script_type> for <purpose> </item> <item> find <asset_type> </item> <item> translate to <language> </item> <item> set theme to <theme> </item> </one-of> </rule> <rule id="asset"> <one-of> crate crates torch torches tree trees npc enemies </one-of> </rule> <rule id="location"> <one-of> castle keep forest path road </one-of> </rule> <rule id="script_type"> <one-of> C# Python blueprint behavior </one-of> </rule> <rule id="language"> <one-of> English Spanish Chinese French </one-of> </rule> </grammar>
This gives a production grammar that NLP models can map to command intents.

# nyghtshade/main.py

import sys


def show_help():
    print("""
    🧠 Nyghtshade CLI
    --------------------------
    Commands:
      scan         → Scan scene/project folder
      place        → Place assets using scene analysis
      gen-script   → Generate code/script via AI
      config       → Configure settings
      help         → Show this help menu
    """)


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        show_help()
        return

    command = sys.argv[1].lower()

    if command == "scan":
        print("🔍 Scanning scene... (placeholder logic)")
    elif command == "place":
        print("📦 Placing assets... (placeholder layout logic)")
    elif command == "gen-script":
        print("🧠 Generating code using AI... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "config":
        print("⚙️  Configuration module not yet implemented")
    else:
        show_help()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

🧪 cli/main.py
import sys

def show_help():
    print("""
    🧠 Nyghtshade CLI
    --------------------------
    Commands:
      scan         → Scan scene/project folder
      place        → Place assets using scene analysis
      gen-script   → Generate code/script via AI
      config       → Configure settings
      help         → Show this help menu
    """)

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        show_help()
        return

    command = sys.argv[1].lower()

    if command == "scan":
        print("🔍 Scanning scene... (placeholder logic)")
    elif command == "place":
        print("📦 Placing assets... (placeholder layout logic)")
    elif command == "gen-script":
        print("🧠 Generating code using AI... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "config":
        print("⚙️  Configuration module not yet implemented")
    else:
        show_help()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    </one-of>
  </rule>
</grammar>

📌 cli/main.py
import sys

def show_help():
    print("""
    🧠 Nyghtshade CLI
    --------------------------
    Commands:
      scan         → Scan scene/project folder
      place        → Place assets using scene analysis
      gen-script   → Generate code/script via AI
      config       → Configure settings
      help         → Show this menu
    """)

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) < 2:
        show_help()
        return

    command = sys.argv[1].lower()

    if command == "scan":
        print("🔍 Scanning scene... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "place":
        print("📦 Placing assets... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "gen-script":
        print("🧠 Generating code... (placeholder)")
    elif command == "config":
        print("⚙️  Configuration module not implemented")
    else:
        show_help()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

🌀 Blender Addon (Python)
bl_info = {
    "name": "Nyghtshade Assistant",
    "blender": (3, 0, 0),
    "category": "AI"
}

import bpy

class NyghtshadePanel(bpy.types.Panel):
    bl_label = "Nyghtshade"
    bl_idname = "NYGHTSHADE_PT_main"
    bl_space_type = 'VIEW_3D'

    def draw(self, context):
        layout = self.layout
        layout.operator("nyghtshade.ask_ai")

class AskAI(bpy.types.Operator):
    bl_idname = "nyghtshade.ask_ai"
    bl_label = "Ask AI"

    def execute(self, context):
        # send scene mesh + prompt
        return {'FINISHED'}

def register():
    bpy.utils.register_class(NyghtshadePanel)
    bpy.utils.register_class(AskAI)

def unregister():
    bpy.utils.unregister_class(NyghtshadePanel)

You said:
how old is the i5-6400 and is it any good for game dev
ChatGPT said:
Not exactly cutting-edge. The Intel Core i5-6400 came out with Intel’s Skylake lineup back in late 2015, which makes it about 10 years old now. (If computer parts aged like fine wine they’d be priceless, but they age like old milk.)

Is it any good for game dev? Here’s the blunt breakdown:

Strengths

Four physical cores (no hyperthreading), which was respectable in 2015.

Decent single-thread performance for basic tasks.

Weaknesses for modern game dev

CPU power is pretty limited by today’s standards. Modern dev tools (Unreal Engine 5, Unity with heavy scenes, shader compilation, baked lighting) love more cores and threads. The i5-6400’s 4 cores/4 threads struggle with that.

No hyperthreading, which means slower compile times and longer build/light bake jobs compared with newer CPUs.

Often paired with slower DDR4 and older platforms without PCIe Gen4, which means slower SSDs, slower GPU bandwidth, and slower overall responsiveness.

Conclusion (straight talk)
It’s fine for learning game dev, coding simple projects, 2D stuff, or lightweight Unity scenes. It can run dev tools, but you’ll be waiting on builds, editor hitches, and slow bakes like it’s camping season and your patience is the tent. For serious 3D development, modern engines, or heavy workflows, you’ll want a newer CPU with more cores and threads.

Basically: It works, but it’s a millstone when you want speed.

Dual channel note
If you’ve got 4 sticks of 4GB each (which sounds like the case), you’ll be running in dual-channel mode, which helps performance compared to a single stick. That’s something you want.

Practical effect for game dev

It’s not fast RAM by today’s standards. Faster memory speeds help a bit with certain game dev tasks, but the bottleneck in your system is the CPU, not the RAM speed.

4GB sticks are small for Unreal/Unity unless you’ve bundled enough of them to get to 16GB or more total RAM. The total capacity matters more than the per-stick speed for loading assets, editing scenes, etc.

Warranty Scope and Compliance Statement (XFX Household Consumer Use)

Pursuant to XFX’s published Limited Hardware Warranty for Household Consumer Use, coverage applies to defects in materials and workmanship for XFX-branded graphics cards purchased within the United States or Canada, provided such products are used in a normal, non-commercial, personal desktop computing environment. “Household use” is expressly defined to include personal gaming and development workloads conducted on an individual consumer’s PC and excludes only enterprise-scale, continuous, or monetized compute operations.

The subject graphics card has not been purchased through a peer-to-peer transaction, auction marketplace, or unauthorized resale channel, nor has it been utilized in any prohibited commercial context, including but not limited to cryptocurrency mining, blockchain computation, render farms, server deployments, clustering, folding operations, or any workload characteristic of sustained 24/7 commercial exploitation. Accordingly, the card’s usage does not fall within any enumerated exclusions set forth in the warranty documentation.

Further, no physical damage has been incurred through improper servicing, modification, or misuse. The warranty expressly permits routine maintenance activities, including thermal compound replacement and heatsink or fan cleaning, without voiding coverage, provided no incidental physical damage results. No components have been fractured, removed, altered, or permanently modified, and no non-reversible alterations have been performed.

With respect to modifications, the card remains in its original factory configuration. No cooling assemblies or components have been replaced, and the product is capable of being returned to XFX in full factory-stock condition, inclusive of all original components, should warranty service be required. As such, no conduct has occurred that would reasonably constitute a basis for warranty termination under the manufacturer’s stated policies.

In summary, the product’s purchase method, usage profile, physical condition, and configuration remain fully compliant with XFX’s published warranty requirements. None of the disqualifying conditions outlined in Section 6 or elsewhere in the warranty guidelines are applicable in this instance.

Thought for 7s
,ZACHARY BINKS — I can’t open that GitHub link from here (no outbound internet in this environment), so I can’t see what’s actually inside your .gitattributes. Humans love making me read files they won’t paste. Classic.

That said, here’s what .gitattributes does and why you should care:

What .gitattributes is
It’s Git’s “how to treat files” rulebook. It controls things like:

Line endings (LF vs CRLF) so Windows doesn’t wage war on Mac/Linux.

Diff behavior (how changes are shown in PRs).

Merge behavior (how conflicts get resolved).

Language stats (what GitHub counts as code).

Binary vs text handling (so Git doesn’t try to diff a PNG like it’s poetry).

LFS rules (if you use Git Large File Storage).

The biggest “real world” use
Stop line-ending chaos:

* text=auto
Git guesses what’s text and normalizes line endings.

*.ps1 text eol=crlf
Keeps PowerShell scripts Windows-friendly.

*.sh text eol=lf
Keeps shell scripts from breaking on Linux.

*.png binary
Prevents dumb diffs and merges on images.

Common patterns you’ll see
Force LF for code:

*.cs text eol=lf

*.cpp text eol=lf

*.h text eol=lf

Treat assets as binary:

*.uasset binary

*.umap binary

*.fbx binary

*.png binary

Custom diffs:

*.md diff=markdown

*.ps1 diff=powershell (sometimes)

GitHub linguist tweaks:

*.h linguist-language=C++

Docs/* linguist-documentation

Why you (especially) should care
With UE5/Unity projects, one wrong .gitattributes and you get:

Massive pointless diffs

“Everything changed” commits

Merge conflicts in files that should never be merged (like .uasset)

Broken scripts from wrong line endings

Do this next (no questions, just instructions)
Paste the contents of your .gitattributes here (just the text). Then I’ll:

Explain exactly what each line does

Tell you what’s risky or redundant

Rewrite it into a “production-grade” version for your repo (especially if it’s game-dev related)

# ============================================
# Neon X Box Message Display
# ============================================

# === COLORS ===
PURPLE='\033[0;35m'
NEON_GREEN='\033[1;32m'
NC='\033[0m'

# === FUNCTION TO PRINT IN NEON X BOX ===
print_neon_box() {
local msg="$1"
local padding=2
local length=${#msg}
local width=$((length + padding * 2))

# Top border
echo -e "${PURPLE}X$(printf '%.0sX' $(seq 1 $width))X${NC}"

# Empty line
echo -e "${PURPLE}X${NC}$(printf ' %.0s' $(seq 1 $width))${PURPLE}X${NC}"

# Message line
echo -e "${PURPLE}X${NC}$(printf ' %.0s' $padding)${NEON_GREEN}${msg}${NC}$(printf ' %.0s' $padding)${PURPLE}X${NC}"

# Empty line
echo -e "${PURPLE}X${NC}$(printf ' %.0s' $(seq 1 $width))${PURPLE}X${NC}"

# Bottom border
echo -e "${PURPLE}X$(printf '%.0sX' $(seq 1 $width))X${NC}"
}

# === USAGE ===
print_neon_box "BRAXTONCONFIG Deployment SUCCESS!"
print_neon_box "All tests passed ✅"
print_neon_box "Git push complete 🚀"

#!/bin/bash
# ============================================
# Smart Deploy with Test Reporting + Auto-Rollback
# Nyghtshade-BraxtonConfig v1.0.0
# ============================================

PROJECT_NAME="Nyghtshade-BraxtonConfig"
VERSION="v1.0.0"
ZIP_FILE="${PROJECT_NAME}_${VERSION}.zip"
GIT_REMOTE_URL="<your-git-url>" # <-- Replace
PINIKO_API_KEY="<your-piniko-api-key>" # <-- Replace
PINIKO_PROJECT_ID="<your-piniko-project-id>" # <-- Replace

rollback_git() {
echo "⏪ Rolling back Git..."
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git push origin main --force
git tag -d "$VERSION"
git push origin :refs/tags/"$VERSION"
}

rollback_piniko() {
echo "⏪ Rolling back Piniko..."
curl -X DELETE "https://api.piniko.com/v1/projects/${PINIKO_PROJECT_ID}/uploads/${VERSION}" \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $PINIKO_API_KEY"
}

# === STEP 1: Unzip Project ===
echo "📂 Unzipping project..."
unzip -o "$ZIP_FILE" -d "$PROJECT_NAME"
cd "$PROJECT_NAME" || { echo "❌ Failed to enter project directory"; exit 1; }

# === STEP 2: Replace 'revolt' with 'BRAXTONCONFIG' ===
echo "🔄 Replacing all occurrences of 'revolt' with 'BRAXTONCONFIG'..."
grep -rl "revolt" . | xargs sed -i '' 's/revolt/BRAXTONCONFIG/g'

# === STEP 3: Run Tests with Detailed Reporting ===
if [ -d "Tests" ]; then
echo "🧪 Running tests with detailed error reporting..."
TEST_FAILED=0
FAILURE_LOG="test_failures.log"
> "$FAILURE_LOG"

for test_file in Tests/*.sh; do
if [ -f "$test_file" ]; then
echo "⚡ Running $test_file..."
bash -n "$test_file" # syntax check first
bash "$test_file" 2>tmp_err.log
EXIT_CODE=$?
if [ $EXIT_CODE -ne 0 ]; then
echo "❌ Test failed: $test_file (Exit code $EXIT_CODE)" | tee -a "$FAILURE_LOG"
awk '{print " " $0}' tmp_err.log >> "$FAILURE_LOG"
TEST_FAILED=1
else
echo "✅ Test passed: $test_file"
fi
rm -f tmp_err.log
fi
done

if [ $TEST_FAILED -ne 0 ]; then
echo "❌ One or more tests failed. Deployment aborted!"
cat "$FAILURE_LOG"
exit 1
fi
else
echo "⚠️ No Tests directory found, skipping tests."
fi

# === STEP 4: Initialize Git Repo ===
echo "🗂 Initializing Git repository..."
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit: ${PROJECT_NAME} ${VERSION}"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin "$GIT_REMOTE_URL"

# === STEP 5: Push to Git ===
echo "🚀 Pushing to Git repository..."
if ! git push -u origin main; then
echo "❌ Git push failed! Aborting."
exit 1
fi

git tag -a "$VERSION" -m "Release ${VERSION} of ${PROJECT_NAME}"
if ! git push origin "$VERSION"; then
echo "❌ Git tag push failed! Rolling back..."
rollback_git
exit 1
fi

# === STEP 6: Upload to Piniko ===
echo "📤 Publishing to Piniko..."
PINIKO_RESPONSE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -X POST \
"https://api.piniko.com/v1/projects/${PINIKO_PROJECT_ID}/uploads" \
-H "Authorization: Bearer $PINIKO_API_KEY" \
-F "file=@../$ZIP_FILE" \
-F "version=$VERSION" \
-F "notes=Release ${VERSION} of ${PROJECT_NAME}")

if [ "$PINIKO_RESPONSE" -ne 200 ]; then
echo "❌ Piniko upload failed! Rolling back Git..."
rollback_git
rollback_piniko
exit 1
fi

echo "✅ Smart deploy complete! All tests passed, Git & Piniko updated safely."

// Single-file scaffold demonstrating RevoltGPT-style integration with Unreal Engine.
// Purpose: educational template for local AI agent integration (HTTP-based).
// NOTE: Replace API_URL and API_KEY with secure config. Do NOT hardcode in production.

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "Modules/ModuleManager.h"
#include "Misc/Paths.h"

// -----------------------------
// Config (replace with secure config, not hardcoded)
// -----------------------------
static const FString REVOLT_API_URL = TEXT("https://your-revoltgpt-server.example/api/v1");
static const FString REVOLT_API_KEY = TEXT("REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_KEY");

// -----------------------------
// Minimal RevoltGPT HTTP wrapper
// -----------------------------
namespace RevoltGPT
{
// Callback signature
using FOnResponse = TFunction<void(bool bSuccess, const FString& ResponseBody)>;

// Helper: POST JSON to endpoint/<path>
static void PostJson(const FString& Path, const FString& JsonPayload, FOnResponse Callback)
{
FString Url = REVOLT_API_URL / Path;
TSharedRef<IHttpRequest, ESPMode::ThreadSafe> Request = FHttpModule::Get().CreateRequest();
Request->SetURL(Url);
Request->SetVerb(TEXT("POST"));
Request->SetHeader(TEXT("Content-Type"), TEXT("application/json"));
Request->SetHeader(TEXT("Authorization"), FString::Printf(TEXT("Bearer %s"), *REVOLT_API_KEY));
Request->SetContentAsString(JsonPayload);
Request->OnProcessRequestComplete().BindLambda([Callback](FHttpRequestPtr Req, FHttpResponsePtr Resp, bool bWasSuccessful)
{
if (!bWasSuccessful || !Resp.IsValid())
{
Callback(false, TEXT("HTTP request failed or invalid response"));
return;
}
Callback(true, Resp->GetContentAsString());
});
Request->ProcessRequest();
}

// Simple synchronous-ish wrapper pattern using async callbacks:
static void Initialize(const FString& Key)
{
// In a real system: store key securely or use secrets manager
// Here we just log
UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("RevoltGPT::Initialize called (key placeholder)"));
}

static void Shutdown()
{
UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("RevoltGPT::Shutdown called"));
}

// Parse file: send file content to agent for indexing/processing (async)
static void ParseFile(const FString& RelativePath, const FString& Content, FOnResponse Callback = nullptr)
{
TSharedPtr<FJsonObject> Obj = MakeShareable(new FJsonObject);
Obj->SetStringField(TEXT("event"), TEXT("parse_file"));
Obj->SetStringField(TEXT("path"), RelativePath);
Obj->SetStringField(TEXT("content"), Content);

FString Payload;
TSharedRef<TJsonWriter<>> Writer = TJsonWriterFactory<>::Create(&Payload);
FJsonSerializer::Serialize(Obj.ToSharedRef(), Writer);
PostJson(TEXT("parse"), Payload, [Callback](bool bOk, const FString& Resp) {
if (Callback) Callback(bOk, Resp);
if (bOk) UE_LOG(LogTemp, Log, TEXT("ParseFile response: %s"), *Resp);
});
}

// Generate text from a prompt
static void GenerateText(const FString& Prompt, FOnResponse Callback)
{
TSharedPtr<FJsonObject> Obj = MakeShareable(new FJsonObject);
Obj->SetStringField(TEXT("prompt"), Prompt);
Obj->SetNumberField(TEXT("max_tokens"), 512);

FString Payload;
TSharedRef<TJsonWriter<>> Writer = TJsonWriterFactory<>::Create(&Payload);
FJsonSerializer::Serialize(Obj.ToSharedRef(), Writer);
PostJson(TEXT("generate"), Payload, Callback);
}

// Implement blueprint / create patch request (server does heavy-lifting)
static void ImplementBlueprint(const FString& BlueprintName, const FString& BlueprintText, FOnResponse Callback = nullptr)
{
TSharedPtr<FJsonObject> Obj = MakeShareable(new FJsonObject);
Obj->SetStringField(TEXT("action"), TEXT("implement_blueprint"));
Obj->SetStringField(TEXT("blueprint_name"), BlueprintName);
Obj->SetStringField(TEXT("blueprint_text"), BlueprintText);

FString Payload;
TSharedRef<TJsonWriter<>> Writer = TJsonWriterFactory<>::Create(&Payload);
FJsonSerializer::Serialize(Obj.ToSharedRef(), Writer);
PostJson(TEXT("implement"), Payload, Callback);
}

// Generic analyze game state
static void AnalyzeGameState(const FString& StateJson, FOnResponse Callback)
{
TSharedPtr<FJsonObject> Obj = MakeShareable(new FJsonObject);
Obj->SetStringField(TEXT("action"), TEXT("analyze_state"));
Obj->SetStringField(TEXT("state_json"), StateJson);

FString Payload;
TSharedRef<TJsonWriter<>> Writer = TJsonWriterFactory<>::Create(&Payload);
FJsonSerializer::Serialize(Obj.ToSharedRef(), Writer);
PostJson(TEXT("analyze"), Payload, Callback);
}
}

// -----------------------------
// RevoltGPT Module (Plugin-like)
// -----------------------------
class FRevoltGPTModule : public IModuleInterface
{
public:
virtual void StartupModule() override
{
RevoltGPT::Initialize(REVOLT_API_KEY);
UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("RevoltGPT module startup - scanning project..."));
ScanProjectFilesAsync();
}

virtual void ShutdownModule() override
{
RevoltGPT::Shutdown();
}

private:
// Asynchronous project scan (fires off ParseFile calls)
void ScanProjectFilesAsync()
{
// Note: scanning Content dir - in large projects optimize and chunk
FString ContentDir = FPaths::ProjectContentDir();
TArray<FString> Files;
IFileManager::Get().FindFilesRecursively(Files, *ContentDir, TEXT("*.*"));

for (const FString& FullPath : Files)
{
FString FileContent;
if (FFileHelper::LoadFileToString(FileContent, *FullPath))
{
// Send relative path for better server indexing
FString RelPath = FullPath;
FPaths::MakePathRelativeTo(RelPath, *FPaths::ProjectDir());
RevoltGPT::ParseFile(RelPath, FileContent, nullptr);
}
}
UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Project scan requests queued (%d files)"), Files.Num());
}
};

IMPLEMENT_MODULE(FRevoltGPTModule, RevoltGPTPlugin)

// -----------------------------
// Utility: Simple JSON helper to extract "text" from model response
// -----------------------------
static bool ExtractGeneratedText(const FString& JsonStr, FString& OutText)
{
TSharedPtr<FJsonObject> Root;
TSharedRef<TJsonReader<>> Reader = TJsonReaderFactory<>::Create(JsonStr);
if (!FJsonSerializer::Deserialize(Reader, Root) || !Root.IsValid()) return false;
if (Root->HasField(TEXT("text")))
{
OutText = Root->GetStringField(TEXT("text"));
return true;
}
// Fallback to data[0].text
if (Root->HasTypedField<EJson::Array>(TEXT("data")))
{
const TArray<TSharedPtr<FJsonValue>> Arr = Root->GetArrayField(TEXT("data"));
if (Arr.Num() && Arr[0].IsValid() && Arr[0]->AsObject()->HasField(TEXT("text")))
{
OutText = Arr[0]->AsObject()->GetStringField(TEXT("text"));
return true;
}
}
return false;
}

#include "Dom/JsonObject.h"
#include "RevoltGPTHttp.h"

namespace RevoltSecure
{
static FString CachedApiKey = TEXT("");

static FString ReadApiKeyFromEnv()
{
// Common name - set this on your system before launching UnrealEditor
FString Key = FPlatformMisc::GetEnvironmentVariable(TEXT("REVOLT_API_KEY"));
return Key;
}

static FString ReadApiKeyFromConfigFile()
{
FString PluginDir = FPaths::Combine(IPluginManager::Get().FindPlugin(TEXT("RevoltGPT"))->GetBaseDir());
FString ConfPath = FPaths::Combine(PluginDir, TEXT("Config/revoltgpt.conf"));

if (!FPaths::FileExists(ConfPath)) return TEXT("");

FString FileContent;
if (!FFileHelper::LoadFileToString(FileContent, *ConfPath)) return TEXT("");

// crude parsing for ApiKey= line
TArray<FString> Lines;
FileContent.ParseIntoArrayLines(Lines);
for (const FString& L : Lines)
{
FString Trim = L.TrimStartAndEnd();
if (Trim.StartsWith(TEXT("ApiKey=")))
{
FString Val = Trim.RightChop(7); // length of "ApiKey="
return Val.TrimStartAndEnd();
}
}
return TEXT("");
}

// call once at startup (safe)
void InitApiKey()
{
if (!CachedApiKey.IsEmpty()) return;

FString Key = ReadApiKeyFromEnv();
if (!Key.IsEmpty())
{
CachedApiKey = Key;
UE_LOG(LogTemp, Display, TEXT("[RevoltSecure] Loaded API key from REVOLT_API_KEY env var"));
return;
}

// fallback (only if env var missing)
Key = ReadApiKeyFromConfigFile();
if (!Key.IsEmpty())
{
CachedApiKey = Key;
UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("[RevoltSecure] Loaded API key from local config (NOT recommended)"));
return;
}

UE_LOG(LogTemp, Error, TEXT("[RevoltSecure] No Revolt API key found. Please set REVOLT_API_KEY env var"));
}

const FString& GetApiKey()
{
return CachedApiKey;
}
} // near top of RevoltGPTHttp.cpp

localhost> # BRAXTONCONFIG Unreal Engine Integration

## Overview

BRAXTONCONFIG is a GitHub project designed to integrate AI models (like GPT, Claude, or Groc) directly into your Unreal Engine project.
It allows **full AI access** to your project files, enabling the AI to understand your game context, implement Blueprints, generate dialogue, create procedural assets, and optimize your project automatically.

This package includes:

- Full Unreal Engine C++ integration
- Blueprint automation examples
- NPC dialogue generation
- Procedural asset generation
- Game state monitoring and optimization

---

## Installation

1. Clone this repository into your Unreal Engine project Plugins folder.
2. Open Unreal Engine and enable the BRAXTONCONFIG plugin in Project Settings → Plugins.
3. Enter your AI API key in the initialization code.

---

## Minute-by-Minute Workflow

### Minute 0:00–1:00 — Project Setup
cpp
#include "BRAXTONCONFIGPlugin.h"
#include "Modules/ModuleManager.h"

class FBRAXTONCONFIGModule : public IModuleInterface
{
public:
virtual void StartupModule() override
{
// Initialize the AI plugin
BRAXTONCONFIG::Initialize("YOUR_API_KEY_HERE");

// Optional logging
UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("BRAXTONCONFIG Plugin Loaded"));

// Scan all project files
ScanProjectFiles();
}

virtual void ShutdownModule() override
{
BRAXTONCONFIG::Shutdown();
}

private:
void ScanProjectFiles()
{
TArray<FString> AllFiles;
FPaths::FindFiles(AllFiles, *FPaths::ProjectContentDir(), TEXT("*.*"));

for (FString File : AllFiles)
{
FString Content;
FFileHelper::LoadFileToString(Content, *File);
BRAXTONCONFIG::ParseFile(File, Content);
}

UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("All files parsed by BRAXTONCONFIG."));
}
};

IMPLEMENT_MODULE(FBRAXTONCONFIGModule, BRAXTONCONFIGPlugin) # BRAXTONCONFIG Unreal Engine Integration

#include "Modules/ModuleManager.h"

class FBRAXTONCONFIGModule : public IModuleInterface
{
public:
virtual void StartupModule() override
{
BRAXTONCONFIG::Initialize("YOUR_API_KEY_HERE");
UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("BRAXTONCONFIG Plugin Loaded"));
ScanProjectFiles();
}

virtual void ShutdownModule() override
{
BRAXTONCONFIG::Shutdown();
}

private:
void ScanProjectFiles()
{
TArray<FString> AllFiles;
FPaths::FindFiles(AllFiles, *FPaths::ProjectContentDir(), TEXT("*.*"));
for (FString File : AllFiles)
{
FString Content;
FFileHelper::LoadFileToString(Content, *File);
BRAXTONCONFIG::ParseFile(File, Content);
}
UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("All project files parsed by BRAXTONCONFIG."));
}
};

IMPLEMENT_MODULE(FBRAXTONCONFIGModule, BRAXTONCONFIGPlugin) #pragma once

## Overview
This project integrates BRAXTONCONFIG AI for ultra-realistic characters, cinematic vehicles, hyper-detailed environments, and physically accurate simulations.

## Features
- AI-driven Blueprints for enemies and NPCs
- Procedural asset generation
- Ultra-realistic character rendering with micro-expressions
- Cinematic vehicle sequences
- Post-combat photorealism (cuts, bruises, blood, etc.)
- Game state monitoring and optimization
- Full support for all BRAXTONCONFIG flags for maximum fidelity

## Setup
1. Clone the repository into Plugins/BRAXTONCONFIG.
2. Enable plugin in Unreal Engine.
3. Insert your API key in BRAXTONCONFIGModule.cpp.
4. Build project and open your level.
5. Use Blueprints or C++ to call BRAXTONCONFIG AI methods.

## Notes
- Minimum resolution: 480x480px
- Use PBR and physically-based lighting
- Avoid filters or stylistic distortion
- All cinematic and character prompts are integrated via system flags BRAXTONCONFIG_Project_UltraRealism/

,ZACHARY BINKS — you’ve got a .gitattributes file that turns into a .gitignore halfway through, then faceplants into a bash script, then keeps going like nothing happened. Git will not “ignore” your feelings about that. It’ll just treat most of that garbage as invalid attributes and quietly do the wrong thing.

Here’s the deal:

What’s valid in your .gitattributes right now
This part is fine:

# Normalize line endings for text files
* text=auto
Everything after that (your Visual Studio ignore rules, node_modules/, Binaries/, etc.) does not belong in .gitattributes. That stuff belongs in .gitignore.

Also: the line

#*.RTF   diff=astextplain. ## Ignore Visual Studio temporary files...
is a smoking gun that two files got smashed together.

What you should use as a clean .gitattributes
Use this. It’s modern, boring, and it prevents the dumbest problems (line endings + binary assets). If you’re doing UE/Unity, this is the baseline you actually want:

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Core: normalize text line endings
# ------------------------------------------------------------
* text=auto

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Explicit line endings for common script types
# ------------------------------------------------------------
*.sh  text eol=lf
*.bash text eol=lf
*.ps1 text eol=crlf
*.bat text eol=crlf
*.cmd text eol=crlf

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Treat common binaries as binary (no diff/merge markers)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
*.png  binary
*.jpg  binary
*.jpeg binary
*.gif  binary
*.webp binary
*.pdf  binary

# Unreal Engine binary assets (VERY important)
*.uasset binary
*.umap   binary

# Archives and executables
*.zip binary
*.7z  binary
*.rar binary
*.exe binary
*.dll binary
*.pdb binary
If you’re mostly C#/Visual Studio, you can also add this (optional):

*.sln      text eol=crlf
*.csproj   text eol=crlf
*.vbproj   text eol=crlf
*.vcxproj  text eol=crlf
What you must do with the rest of that giant block
Move all the “ignore Visual Studio temporary files, build results…” stuff into a file named:

✅ .gitignore

That entire chunk is a classic VisualStudio.gitignore template and it’s valid there.

Why this matters (in real life)
Putting ignore rules in .gitattributes does nothing (except confuse Git and you).

Marking .uasset/.umap as binary prevents Git from trying to “merge” them and corrupting them.

Line-ending rules stop “every file changed” commits when switching machines.

Quick cleanup checklist
Replace .gitattributes with the clean version above.

Create/replace .gitignore with the Visual Studio ignore block you pasted (starting at ## Ignore Visual Studio temporary files...).

Commit both.

That’s it. Git is now slightly less of a chaotic gremlin.

Here’s what a .gitattributes file generally is and why projects include one so you’re not left staring at a mystery file in your own repo instead of actually working on game code:

What a .gitattributes file does

It tells Git how to treat specific files or patterns in the repository. 
w3schools.com

Common uses include:

Forcing consistent line endings across different operating systems (windows vs mac/linux). 
w3schools.com

Marking certain files as binary (so Git doesn’t try weird diffs or merges). 
GitHub

Enabling Git LFS handling for large assets (models, textures, audio). 
GitHub

Setting merge/diff behavior for special file types. 
Stack Overflow

Controlling export-ignore for Git archive exports. 
Half-Elf Tech

Basic syntax

Each line is a pattern + attributes:

*.png   binary
*.txt   text eol=lf
pattern matches filenames or file types.

Attributes after the pattern tell Git what to apply. 
Ken Muse

Why there’s one in that repo
Even tiny or placeholder repos sometimes include a .gitattributes to standardize line endings or ensure part of GitHub’s language stats doesn’t miscount assets. If you look at other repos (like template lists), they often include a baseline .gitattributes.

backup current files → Saved/BraxtonConfigBackups/<timestamp>/...

write new files

verify written hashes

if anything fails → restore backup (rollback)

# Braxton Config Download Plugin (UE5)

A UE5 Editor plugin that downloads, validates, versions, and applies configuration packages per-project.

## Features
- List projects from a config dashboard (or local registry)
- Upload configuration packages (manifest + zip)
- Download & apply config packages to a UE5 project
- Hash validation (SHA-256)
- Automatic backup + rollback on failure

## Installation
1. Copy this folder into: YourProject/Plugins/BraxtonConfigDownloadPlugin/
2. Regenerate project files (if needed)
3. Enable the plugin in **Edit → Plugins**
4. Restart the editor

## Usage
- Open: **Tools → Braxton Config Manager**
- Select a project
- Pick a config package version
- Click **Download & Apply**
- Roll back via **Restore Previous** (uses Saved backups)

## Config Package Format
Each package is a .zip containing:
- manifest.json
- files/ (relative paths)

See: Docs/ConfigPackageFormat.md

## Roadmap
- Auth (API tokens)
- Per-project permissions
- Diff view for ini changes
- Scheduled “check for updates”
- Optional CLI for CI/CD

4) Source/BraxtonConfigDownloadPlugin/Private/BraxtonConfigDownloadPluginModule.cpp
#include "BraxtonConfigDownloadPluginModule.h"

#include "ToolMenus.h"
#include "LevelEditor.h"
#include "Widgets/Docking/SDockTab.h"
#include "Widgets/Layout/SBox.h"
#include "Widgets/Text/STextBlock.h"
#include "Framework/Docking/TabManager.h"

static const FName BraxtonConfigTabName(TEXT("BraxtonConfigManager"));

#define LOCTEXT_NAMESPACE "FBraxtonConfigDownloadPluginModule"

void FBraxtonConfigDownloadPluginModule::StartupModule()
{
    // Register tab
    FGlobalTabmanager::Get()->RegisterNomadTabSpawner(
        BraxtonConfigTabName,
        FOnSpawnTab::CreateLambda([](const FSpawnTabArgs& Args)
        {
            return SNew(SDockTab)
                .TabRole(ETabRole::NomadTab)
                [
                    SNew(SBox)
                    .Padding(16.0f)
                    [
                        SNew(STextBlock)
                        .Text(LOCTEXT("BraxtonConfigWindowText",
                            "Braxton Config Manager\n\nNext: add Project list + Upload/Download + Apply + Rollback."))
                    ]
                ];
        })
    .SetDisplayName(LOCTEXT("BraxtonConfigTabTitle", "Braxton Config Manager"))
    .SetMenuType(ETabSpawnerMenuType::Hidden);

    // Register menu
    UToolMenus::RegisterStartupCallback(
        FSimpleMulticastDelegate::FDelegate::CreateRaw(this, &FBraxtonConfigDownloadPluginModule::RegisterMenus)
    );
}

void FBraxtonConfigDownloadPluginModule::ShutdownModule()
{
    if (UToolMenus::IsToolMenusAvailable())
    {
        UToolMenus::UnRegisterStartupCallback(this);
    }

    FGlobalTabmanager::Get()->UnregisterNomadTabSpawner(BraxtonConfigTabName);
}

void FBraxtonConfigDownloadPluginModule::RegisterMenus()
{
    UToolMenu* Menu = UToolMenus::Get()->ExtendMenu("LevelEditor.MainMenu.Tools");
    if (!Menu) return;

    FToolMenuSection& Section = Menu->AddSection("BraxtonConfigSection", LOCTEXT("BraxtonConfigSection", "Braxton"));

    Section.AddMenuEntry(
        "OpenBraxtonConfigManager",
        LOCTEXT("OpenBraxtonConfigManagerLabel", "Braxton Config Manager"),
        LOCTEXT("OpenBraxtonConfigManagerTooltip", "Open the Braxton Config Manager window."),
        FSlateIcon(),
        FUIAction(FExecuteAction::CreateRaw(this, &FBraxtonConfigDownloadPluginModule::OpenPluginWindow))
    );
}

void FBraxtonConfigDownloadPluginModule::OpenPluginWindow()
{
    FGlobalTabmanager::Get()->TryInvokeTab(BraxtonConfigTabName);
}

#undef LOCTEXT_NAMESPACE

IMPLEMENT_MODULE(FBraxtonConfigDownloadPluginModule, BraxtonConfigDownloadPlugin)

,ZACHARY BINKS — I can’t open that GitHub link from here (no outbound internet in this environment), so I can’t see what’s actually inside your .gitattributes. Humans love making me read files they won’t paste. Classic.
That said, here’s what .gitattributes does and why you should care:
What .gitattributes is
It’s Git’s “how to treat files” rulebook. It controls things like:
Line endings (LF vs CRLF) so Windows doesn’t wage war on Mac/Linux.
Diff behavior (how changes are shown in PRs).
Merge behavior (how conflicts get resolved).
Language stats (what GitHub counts as code).
Binary vs text handling (so Git doesn’t try to diff a PNG like it’s poetry).
LFS rules (if you use Git Large File Storage).
The biggest “real world” use
Stop line-ending chaos:
* text=autoGit guesses what’s text and normalizes line endings.
*.ps1 text eol=crlfKeeps PowerShell scripts Windows-friendly.
*.sh text eol=lfKeeps shell scripts from breaking on Linux.
*.png binaryPrevents dumb diffs and merges on images.
Common patterns you’ll see
Force LF for code:
*.cs text eol=lf
*.cpp text eol=lf
*.h text eol=lf
Treat assets as binary:
*.uasset binary
*.umap binary
*.fbx binary
*.png binary
Custom diffs:
*.md diff=markdown
*.ps1 diff=powershell (sometimes)
GitHub linguist tweaks:
*.h linguist-language=C++

Why you (especially) should care
With UE5/Unity projects, one wrong .gitattributes and you get:
Massive pointless diffs
“Everything changed” commits
Merge conflicts in files that should never be merged (like .uasset)
Broken scripts from wrong line endings
Do this next (no questions, just instructions)
Paste the contents of your .gitattributes here (just the text). Then I’ll:
Explain exactly what each line does
Tell you what’s risky or redundant
Rewrite it into a “production-grade” version for your repo (especially if it’s game-dev related)

ChatGPT said:
,ZACHARY BINKS — you’ve got a .gitattributes file that turns into a .gitignore halfway through, then faceplants into a bash script, then keeps going like nothing happened. Git will not “ignore” your feelings about that. It’ll just treat most of that garbage as invalid attributes and quietly do the wrong thing.
Here’s the deal:
What’s valid in your .gitattributes right now
This part is fine:
# Normalize line endings for text files * text=auto
Everything after that (your Visual Studio ignore rules, node_modules/, Binaries/, etc.) does not belong in .gitattributes. That stuff belongs in .gitignore.
Also: the line
#*.RTF diff=astextplain. ## Ignore Visual Studio temporary files...
is a smoking gun that two files got smashed together.
What you should use as a clean .gitattributes
Use this. It’s modern, boring, and it prevents the dumbest problems (line endings + binary assets). If you’re doing UE/Unity, this is the baseline you actually want:
# ------------------------------------------------------------ # Core: normalize text line endings # ------------------------------------------------------------ * text=auto # ------------------------------------------------------------ # Explicit line endings for common script types # ------------------------------------------------------------ *.sh text eol=lf *.bash text eol=lf *.ps1 text eol=crlf *.bat text eol=crlf *.cmd text eol=crlf # ------------------------------------------------------------ # Treat common binaries as binary (no diff/merge markers) # ------------------------------------------------------------ *.png binary *.jpg binary *.jpeg binary *.gif binary *.webp binary *.pdf binary # Unreal Engine binary assets (VERY important) *.uasset binary *.umap binary # Archives and executables *.zip binary *.7z binary *.rar binary *.exe binary *.dll binary *.pdb binary
If you’re mostly C#/Visual Studio, you can also add this (optional):
*.sln text eol=crlf *.csproj text eol=crlf *.vbproj text eol=crlf *.vcxproj text eol=crlf
What you must do with the rest of that giant block
Move all the “ignore Visual Studio temporary files, build results…” stuff into a file named:
✅ .gitignore
That entire chunk is a classic VisualStudio.gitignore template and it’s valid there.
Why this matters (in real life)
Putting ignore rules in .gitattributes does nothing (except confuse Git and you).
Marking .uasset/.umap as binary prevents Git from trying to “merge” them and corrupting them.
Line-ending rules stop “every file changed” commits when switching machines.
Quick cleanup checklist
Replace .gitattributes with the clean version above.
Create/replace .gitignore with the Visual Studio ignore block you pasted (starting at ## Ignore Visual Studio temporary files...).
Commit both.
That’s it. Git is now slightly less of a chaotic gremlin.

# Auto detect text files and perform LF normalization * text=auto

# Auto detect text files and perform LF normalization * text=auto
What that line does (in plain English)
Git will auto-detect text files
It will normalize line endings in the repo to LF (so your diffs don’t explode just because Windows exists)
When someone checks out on Windows, Git can still give them CRLF locally depending on their config, but the repo stays sane
What you should add (because reality)
If you touch Unreal/Unity assets or scripts, add these so Git doesn’t try to “merge” binary files like an idiot:
# Scripts: keep them from breaking *.sh text eol=lf *.ps1 text eol=crlf *.bat text eol=crlf *.cmd text eol=crlf # Unreal binary assets *.uasset binary *.umap binary # Common binaries *.png binary *.jpg binary *.jpeg binary *.gif binary *.zip binary *.pdf binary

Here’s what a .gitattributes file generally is and why projects include one so you’re not left staring at a mystery file in your own repo instead of actually working on game code:

What a .gitattributes file does

It tells Git how to treat specific files or patterns in the repository. 
w3schools.com

Common uses include:

Forcing consistent line endings across different operating systems (windows vs mac/linux). 
w3schools.com

Marking certain files as binary (so Git doesn’t try weird diffs or merges). 
GitHub

Enabling Git LFS handling for large assets (models, textures, audio). 
GitHub

Setting merge/diff behavior for special file types. 
Stack Overflow

Controlling export-ignore for Git archive exports. 
Half-Elf Tech

Basic syntax

Each line is a pattern + attributes:

*.png   binary
*.txt   text eol=lf
pattern matches filenames or file types.

Attributes after the pattern tell Git what to apply. 
Ken Muse

Why there’s one in that repo
Even tiny or placeholder repos sometimes include a .gitattributes to standardize line endings or ensure part of GitHub’s language stats doesn’t miscount assets. If you look at other repos (like template lists), they often include a baseline .gitattributes. 
GitHub

If you want to see the actual text in that specific file, you can open the “Raw” button in your browser on GitHub or tell me to fetch just the contents and I’ll pull it and paste it for you.
